"Let there be a time in the future, I prayed, when he laughs with his children, and plays on the shore with them, and spends all his nights in loving arms. Let us have that. To whom I was praying I did not know. The future was in our own hands. If we wanted a world where such things were possible, it was for us to make it." 
 I have read a number of sequels this year that have let me down. Second book syndrome, third book syndrome, you name it. Generally, if I like the first book in the series, the subsequent ones will be lacking in some sense. Usually the fault lies within characterization. The first book generally develops the character, and all the development stops as soon as the second book begins. A good plot is always more than welcome, but it takes a hell of a lot more than that to develop a good story. I have been a long-time fan of Juliet Marillier; she has always a masterful storyteller and writer, and I am pleased to say that this book is an excellent continuation of this series. I don't think I need to say much on the quality of her writing; if you have read any of her previous books, you will know that Juliet Marillier's writing is beautiful, evocative, while avoiding the trap of being Dickensianly verbose. Her dialogue is believable, her dialects beautifully done, and written so well that despite their pervasiveness, I have no cause for complaints. 
 Let me digress for a bit while we're on the topic of dialects; in a lot of romance novels involving Irish or Scottish characters, the local dialect is more often than not, intolerable. Laughable. A mockery. They're of the Willie-the-Groundskeeper bent, if you need a little The Simpsons reference in your day. Ach! Ye ken, lassie. Ah, dinna fash yerself, laddie., and so on, and so forth. More often than not, such portrayal of Celtic dialects have me wincing and wondering why the collective countries of Scotland and Ireland do not issue some sort of ultimatum to romance writers everywhere involving the portrayal of their people's speech. 
 While the dialect of the Little People, the Good Folk, the Fey Folk, whatever you want to call them, is almost aurally transcribed, it is so well-done and so consistently done, that I find no reason to roll my eyes at all. The speech, the accent, the distinctive ways of speaking all feels completely in tune with the book's setting and characters. For example: 
 "'Guards?' Steep spoke with derision. 'Ye mean them in the ha'? Just for show, they are, save for the Twa. The real fighters, we're a' doon below. We're the strong backbone o' this place; wi'oot the likes o' us, wha'd keep the Southies in check?'" 
 Back to the meat of the book itself. This book is about learning, bravery, sacrifice. About overcoming your own principles and morals for the greater good. About surrending your own short-term wishes and dreams for the chance at a brighter future. About hope, about holding on to that hope when all seems lost. Lest I give the wrong impression about this book because of my high praises, this book is not saccharine sweet. There is no such thing as saccharine sweetness in a Juliet Marillier novel. The events in this book is harsh, unforgiving; life is difficult, people die, friends and strangers alike. There is no such thing as a "safe" character in this series. Beware to whom you get attached, because you might lose them. Still, life goes on, and the living must continue to live and fight and save the mourning for another day. There is no time for mourning, no time for weakness, because the enemy will use that weakness against you, given an iota of a chance. 
 This is not a standalone book, it is very much a continuation of a series, and while there is a small bit of summary of previous events, you will be hopelessly lost if you have not read the first book. In Raven Flight, Neryn continues her life with the rebel, but her training does not last long. As a Caller, her role is bigger than that. She has to seek and summon a number of Guardians, among them the Master of Shadows, the Hag of Isles, the Lord of the North. She has to travel quickly and lightly, so her sole bodyguard and companion is the imminently capable (albeit pricklier than a cactus), Tali. Along the way, they meet old friends, as well as the Good Folk, and encounter plenty of trouble along the way. The pacing is quick, the plot moves quickly and rationally. In other sequels, the action-packed plot still manage to bore me to tears because of the lack of character development. Not so here. 
 The most prominent characters in this book are the traveling companions of Neryn and Tali. Neryn is still weak, still overly soft. She is very human, despite what she has seen, despite what she has suffered, with high morals that bothered me at times. Neryn is powerful, but she is soft. She is reluctant to join the fight, even if she knows that's what is needed to win the war. 
 "It's going to be a long, hard fight, and people are going to die. You should know that, Neryn. What's needed here isn't soft dreams of true love. It's anger--the anger that drives a person forward. The fury that keeps them fighting right up to the moment the knife goes in. In our world there's no place for love." 
 Her rebel friends constantly remind her that she cannot afford such crises of conscience, that death is a necessity, that her gift is meant to be used, but Neryn is still frustratingly reluctant to use it, because she remembers how her power can kill as well. She has killed before, for the greater good; if she had not done what she did, even more rebel lives would have been lost, but Neryn is so stricken with her guilt that she can hardly bear to use her power of calling on the Good Folk in times of need. 
 "'Still weighed down by conscience? Even though what you did saved both our lives? Neryn, the rebellion depends on your gift. Without you, there's no chance we can do it in the time we have. You need to put these scruples behind you; if you can't, they'll become a burden too heavy for you to carry.'" 
 In the previous book, we met the prickly, antagonistic, permanently angry Tali. I didn't like her very much at first then, but her character is built up so much more in this book. It seemed to be a bad idea to throw Tali and Neryn together at first, and I questioned Regan's decision of assigning her to be Neryn's guard...so did Tali. She has been training Neryn, but in her mind, Neryn is still a weak, incompetent girl, ill-equipped to do what she must do to save them all. Her first impression of Neryn is not a positive one, she thought Neryn was "a wee girl wandering where she didn't belong, trying to do a job that was far too big for her. A girl who hadn't the first idea what kind of life she'd need to live if she became one of Regan's Rebels." 
 Tali is still strong, but she shows her more vulnerable side as we get to know her, and I came to love her as a foil for the oftentimes weak, soft-hearted Neryn. Tali is straightforward, she speaks her mind, she takes no prisoners, there is no bullshitting her. She does not coddle Neryn at all, she cuts Neryn no slack for her physical and mental weakness, and she is exactly what Neryn needs. She became my favorite character in this book. Tali has feelings, she loves deeply, but she knows to keep her emotions under wraps, because that is just hoping for too much. All she can hope for day by day is survival. Anything else is just a pipe dream. 
 "I have no children. I never will. I have no husband, no lover, no family. Only fellow rebels, others like me. All of them understand how it has to be. Hard. Cruel. Brutal. Full of choices like the one Andra had to face. That makes it all the more vital to keep what we do under strict control." 
 I have gone on for so long in this review, gushing about this book for a reason. Read this series. Read this book.

The telling of the story of their time in the Congo (and dealing with their overbearing father) alternates between all four of the girls' points of view, plus occasionally their mother's POV is added in, but from the "current" day, looking back, whereas the girls' points of view are told from the time they are there.

What kind of ending was that?? The book just ended, in a place I felt it should have continued from. There really wasn't anything major that happened.

 Cat is a Soothsayer who is predicting futures and reading truths as part of her act for a circus. Unbeknownst to her she is being watched by Beta Sinte (I think that's the right spelling). Beta Sinte is part of the new family in charge of Sinte, and he wants Cat...for some reason she can't fathom, aside from her Kingmaker abilities. As the story progresses, so do Cat and Griffin's (Beta Sinte) closeness. But Cat is worried about the people who she's been running from the past 8 years, and we expect her problems to catch up with her soon. 
 Griffin is number two only to Alpha Sinte, his sister. He enlists Cat's help to get his sisters and family ready for the gathering of nobles at a dinner party.  I enjoyed how the story weaves in the Greek gods and Greek mythology I'm totally a sucker for that sort of thing. (See Daughters of the Moon for short YA novels.) I enjoyed the stories behind certain things and seeing how their world works. This is definitely a fantasy novel more than paranormal, but I don't currently have a fantasy shelf so I can't tag it that way, but there's magic and dragons and things like that so it's definitely something awesome to read. Cat's character is strong and you want her to succeed especially when you hear about her childhood. It simply broke my heart. The things done to her awful. But Griffin, oh Griffin, he is a great H. I really do like his character and he is definitely swoon worthy. 
 I did however feel that there wasn't a climax in this book, no big event aside from  Cat almost dying from a knife wound from Daphne, we knew she'd be a problem, should have done something sooner. Which I found a little silly, that of all the things that happen to Cat this is what takes her down? There were a few other points like when Griffin also got injured and almost died....  but aside from those things I didn't really feel like that was a significant transition into the story. And where the book ended? Well that wasn't exactly an ending, I didn't feel like it was a stopping place, I didn't feel like I concluded something. I'm still waiting for Cat to tell Griffin AND us who she really is. Out loud. And she hasn't, so there was no conclusion for me. I know it's a Chronicle so maybe that's how these things work, but for me I knocked off a star for that. Otherwise I didn't really find anything wrong with the book. The pacing was great, the writing well worded, and I devoured the book in a day. I'd say it's a great book to read, and I look forward to reading the next installment.

1.5 stars 
 This book's premise had the potential for success: 
 Mysterious new guys? Check. 
 Demons? Check. 
 Angels? Check. 
 Past lives coming back to haunt you? Check. 
 Unfortunately, all the author's good intentions went downhill with the poor execution and bland writing. It didn't help that from the first chapter, I felt like I was reading an alternate version of Fallen by Lauren Kate, with a Twilight-esque feel to it. The plot was so predictable. It also didn't help that the heroine was really boring. I couldn't tell her friends apart either, and I suspect that without the dialogue tags, our special heroine would be indistinguishable from her friends. 
 The narrative was just clumsy, at times giving me a rundown of everything the heroine was doing. The way that the author kept alluding to the heroine's interest in archeology to explain away her obsession with the past was awkward. You could tell the author only did it because she needed some way to tie in the memories of a past life to the story. A plot-device. Sadly, in a more experienced author's hands, this interest in archeology could have really worked. Heck, even without the archeological interest, it could have still really worked. But the author only mentioned it when she felt she really needed to. It felt forced. 
 Not only that, the main character's deduction of reasoning was really flawed and only suited the author's needs. In other words, our heroine lives in and grew up in a non-fantasy world. She has no belief or introduction in the supernatural, so her leaps of logic to supernatural causes are unbelievable. For example,  her best friend commits attempted suicide. Earlier, our special heroine saw said best friend talking with handsome new guy. Therefore, new guy must be somehow responsible for the suicide attempt.  Outrageous, right? 
 But that's not all that was wrong with this book. Here come the Twilight allusions: Instalove with the hero, hero's surly personality resembling one sparkly vampire's, interactions with supernatural characters in mundane settings (high school (again. Sigh.), lunchroom, English class, the car, a forest, a restaurant interrogation), obsession with the hero, heroine having no distinct personality of her own, heroine lives with her absentee, divorced parent (the mother--the father lives far away), forbidden love, and blah, blah, blah. Oh! And did I mention this all takes place in Seattle? (Ahem, how far is Forks again?) 
 No, those settings and themes don't distinctly belong to Twilight, but you read those scenes and TELL me they don't have the "inspired by Twilight" feel to them. 
 Furthermore, the author's attempt at making Damiel (the other new guy) seem creepy and suave at the same time were so in-your-face gauche. It had the I'm attracted to you, now I'm creeped out by you, now I'm attracted to you again, oops--I forgot I felt creeped out by you feel to it. 
 I kept reading the book, all the way to the end, waiting for it to surprise me. But it didn't. It helped that I had low expectations from the get go (ie. no disappointment). Maybe the very small twist at the end (to clarify, I mean the fact that the nephilim birthed in the heroine's previous life was actually Damiel's son ) might count as the surprise, but it hardly stood up against the weight of the rest of the book. Perhaps that twist was what inspired the author, because briefly while she was writing it, those passages had more life to them. But, as I said, it just doesn't stand up to the rest of the book. 
 There were so many places where the author could have developed the story further. Fatima (the minor psychic character in the story) was given a really small role, which was for plot convenience, of course, but she could have been developed into a strong secondary character--something beyond a plot-device. Near the end, the author played around with the theme of absolute forgiveness of absolute evil, but it lost its effect because it wasn't running in the background of the story from the beginning. It didn't help that Damiel was a flat character. If he was a complex character, then the theme could have been played up from the beginning. But it failed. 
 In conclusion, I don't recommend this novel unless you're some kind of Twilight/Fallen addict and miss those books so much you need more of the same, or you've never read a book before in your life (then this book will sure surprise you). This book regurgitated things we've seen done before, and done a million times over in this subgenre. The author didn't bring anything new to the angel-demon subgenre and didn't add her own personal touch to give it a fresh perspective. YA fantasy fans, look elsewhere for your next read.

Reaction to the cover and synopsis: The cover is beautiful! I loved the font. The title is bigger than the author's name so it draws more attention. I hate when it is the other way around. Gives off a vibe that it is going to be a thriller. 
 The synopsis really doesn't explain much. Just that it is a post-apocalyptic story about a girl named Mary. She lives in a village sourronded by the forest of hands and teeth and are worried about something called the unconsecrated. And that there is a Sisterhood and the guardians. 
 My Summary:We are seeing things through Mary's eyes. When her mother is bitten and sent to be with the unconsecrated her brother is angry and sends her off to join the Sisterhood. Mary has not been claimed by a man to be married and he refuses to let her stay with him another year to give her more time. Unclaimed women will become Sisters in the Sisterhood. The Sisterhood watch over the village and guide them. They make the rules. 
 Mary is put under silence until she reads the scripture, a huge book that holds the holy word, five times. During her silence one of her best friends, Travis, comes in. He is injured. The Sisters aren't sure if he will make it. Mary sits with him a night and tells him of a world outside of the village. She tells him about how her mother used to tell her that there was an ocean out there. Where there was nothing but water as far as the eye could see. She was still under silence, but the head Sister believed she was praying for Travis. She ended up falling in love with Travis. 
 Travis is meant to marry Mary's best friend Cas, who comes to see Travis as well. Along with his brother Harry. All four have been friends since they were young. 
 Harry claims Mary and they are to be married with Travis and Cass. The ceremony takes a week to complete. Travis promises Mary he will come for her. To find a way to be with her. But before the end of the week there is a breach on the village. The Fast One (who I did not explain, because it wouldn't be nice to ruin the entire thing.) got into the village. Now the entire village is under attack. 
 Mary, Travis, Cass, Harry, Jed(Mary's brother), Jacob(a small boy), Beth(Jed's wife), and Mary's dog are the only ones to make it out and onto a path to safety. But now they are stuck in this area that was once forbidden by the sisterhood with little food and water and no sense of direction. 
 My review: It was well written. I really liked that. But let me start off by saying that if you are looking for a romance, you might not want to pick up this book. Although on the front of the book it says it is a romance, there really isn't a lot of romantic moments captured in this book. She tries to, but for me it didn't catch. Don't get me wrong, Mary has one truly moving moment with Travis that had me balling, but that was it for romance. 
 Thrilling? You betca. This book really keeps you on your toes. I wasn't able to put it down once I got out of the village. I had to finish it. I had to know if they found their way, if there really was an ocean. Which is silly, I know, because I KNOW there is an ocean. But nobody but Mary believed that there was. 
 So why 3 stars if it was so amazing? I am sorry to say, but this book falls under the 'annoying main character' category for me. Which I am finding a lot of the new releases are lately. Mary never seems happy with anything. Even when she has what she says she wants, she is never satisfied. It really struck home with me when she was sharing a house with Travis, hiding from the unconsecrated and was avoiding him. I found that selfish. Where I know it was supposed to come across as ambitious and show her hope, it just came across as her being a bitch. And that happened a lot during this book. 
 Another character I didn't care for was her brother. He wasn't very well rounded and a found him a bit unrealistic. 
 Other than that her characters were fine. My favorite had to be the dog. 
 Will I read the second: I am not sure if I will pick up the second book to this. I wasn't satisfied with the ending and there is nothing she can do to make that better. So I am not for sure if I will even think it is worth reading. I am going to give it a little bit of time. But I will review it if I do change my mind and decide to pick it up.

The only person there who doesn't seem to think she's crazy (which Mara is convinced she is) is Noah Shaw, British bad-boy with an ultra-bad reputation. As if things couldn't get any weirder, Mara starts envisioning the deaths of people she hates: A man abusing his dog, her horrible Spanish teacher...and then the deaths happen. Just as she imagines them. As Mara gets closer to Noah, she starts having dreams that help her remember what happened the night of the accident. But then she learns something about Noah that changes everything.

 "I gracelessly darted into the crowd and only narrowly avoided being elbowed in the face by a girl attired in what could only be described as 'slutty Gryffindor' apparel." (142).

What, are you afraid I'll ruin the image you're cultivating here?" "What image," I said flatly. "Angsty, solitary, introspective emoteen, staring off into the distance as she sketches withered leaves falling from bare branches and..." Noah's voice trailed off, but the look of cool amusement on his face didn't. "No, that was lovely. Please continue." (119). I loved Noah and Mara's banter. They always had the most entertaining conversations. 
 This book certainly had its creepy moments too, so those looking for paranormal will not be disappointed. 
 All in all, a really fabulous read. I cannot wait for the sequel!

This is really a tale of the American dream told through a family that had immigrated to America from Cameroon. It's set in the late 2000s, around the time of the economic collapse, and it tells the tale of how different families dealt with good times and with bad ones, and how they approached life looking to grasp those hard-sought American dreams.

This book is so much more than a dual biography! By reading this book, you will learn about the state of Russia in the early 20th century, the beginning of World War I, the mystery of the starets called Rasputin, hemophilia and everything else needed to understand the lives of Nicholas and Alexandra Romanov. 
 Despite some sudden back-and-forth jumps, it was almost like watching a movie. 
 Now having read the book, I really want to point a finger at Alexandra and say it's all her fault, but I've forced myself to look at all the given facts and have come to a conclusion: It could've happened to anyone, really. Is it really her fault that she was disastrously stubborn, opinionated, and selfish? Any mother who had to watch her own son in pain and on the verge of death as often as she did could've acquired these traits, right? No? Maybe? And Nicolas? He was just too naive, kind and in love. They were dealt a certain hand in life, and they didn't play it properly. 
 Having earned the name "Nicolas the Bloody" because he sent millions of men to their deaths in the first World War, and his wife Alexandra "the German woman", are two of the most misunderstood people in history. Massie succeeded in painting a different, more intimate and true picture of just two incredibly naive people in love who did what they thought was necessary in order to protect their family.
I read this so long ago that i cant remember much, but i liked it enough to go buy the sequel...which ive yet to read...ill give this a better review once ive reread it...

4.1 ratings? I really don't get it. The plot was so poorly thought and there were times when I was convinced that two different people wrote this thing on their own and then just stitched those pages together. Half of it doesn't even make sense. Emily doesn't make sense and Logan, you're just a fuck-up. Don't finish crappy books.

 I have soft spot for books that are not set in the US or England and when I found out that this one is set in Burma, I knew I have to read it. It was a good decision, The Art of Hearing Heartbeats changed my life forever that I am now confident enough to declare that I am romance reader. 
 The love story on Mi Mi and Tin Win brought me to an emotional roller coaster and to tell you the truth, this is the best romance I have read in entire life. 
 Thank you, Mr. Sendker for writing such a beautiful story. Thank you for using your talent to touch my heart, crush it to pieces while on the other hand, making it such a lovely reading experience.

This was not a bad book, but for some r Eason I just couldn't get into it. It was interesting the whole time, the characters were great and well written. But for some reason I can not explain I did not find myself on the edge of my seat anxious to know what happens next. I kept putting this book down and picking up other ones. I would recommend trying this book to others and that's why it's getting a three instead of a two.

5 stars for being the best YA "romance" book I've ever read. For its genre, it shines. It's such a relief to read a book with characters like Eleanor and Park who are real, good, full people. I can't love them enough. They give me hope. 
 Eleanor's situation was a little too forced, and the ending - meh. But I'm maintaining the 5 stars for Rainbow Rowell's bravery in writing such a book.

This book was enjoyable, really, it was fun. BUT what made me hate it was the Italian, it was so stale and felt forced and unreal. Nico's mother sounded like a robotic cliche dispenser, I'm not even sure if half the stuff was correct, all I know is from what I read in Italian and from Italian literature, NO ONE speaks like that and it's just annoying as hell, made me hate the book.

I don't know why, but this one didn't connect with me as much as the first two in the series did. :( Does that make me crazy? Maybe a little bit (or a LOTTA bit!) considering that this one is a million times less dark than the first two. 
 Even though this was told completely from Caleb's first person point of view and CJ Roberts did an awesome job with it, it just didn't feel like Caleb to me. He wasn't the character we grew to know in the first two books; he didn't act or think like someone with his past ever could. Not because he wasn't as twisted -- because he definitely had his fair share of Caleb-worthy comments that were admittedly what I was looking for! -- but because nothing that he thought or said or did seemed to be who he was. After twenty-seven years of being who he was, it seemed so easy for him to flip a switch and think COMPLETELY different. To be someone more vulnerable than even the nicest guys I've read about. 
 And it felt so forced to me. Like the author was trying to make him witty and sarcastic because it's a popular quality in book boys now (and she succeeded!). Maybe if this was simply another book about two characters I didn't know yet then I'd have loved this, but after just finishing the first two literally within the past few days, it doesn't feel anything like the characters I knew at all, or even characters that they could've grown to be so fast, so soon. 
 STILL. If you liked the first two books, then you definitely won't want to miss out on Epilogue! I don't think I'll ever get enough of being able to get a glimpse into the male mind ;) And I love knowing that Livvie and Caleb -- or Sophia and James -- get to have their HEA of sorts <3

Sub-genre: Dr. Who 
 Literary conflict: ??? 
 GOOD: 
 Solid editing/polish: 
 Fun characters: 
 Witty repartee: 
 Great "how-it-works" technology descriptions: - 
 Great ending: - 
 Thought provoking: - 
 BAD: 
 Rapid head-hopping: 
 Huge cast of characters: 
 Unbelievable moments: - 
 I found the POV, third-person omniscient, rather distracting. The point of view changes from one sentence to the next and that really jerked me out of the story. If the switch happened at chapter boundaries, it would be better. Worse, the "head hopping" from the thoughts of one character to another included several characters ay the beginning of the story, but only a couple at the end. What was the purpose then? I suffered through the maze of all those thoughts at the start when nothing was happening but never got to know how they felt at the end about how it all turned out. 
 The conflict is not spelled out well at all. Is it man vs. man or man vs. nature?  I consider it man vs. nature because the "bad guys", for the most part, only show up at the beginning and then are never seen again. By the time I realized the bad guys weren't coming back, the story was almost over.  
 I have read a great deal of Michael Moorcock's books. He effectively took his back story for his other series like Elric or Eternal Champion and stuck the Doctor in the middle of it. Perhaps a Dr. Who fan might not be troubled by that if they hadn't read Moorcock's other works, but it doesn't really fit well with the Dr. Who universe anyway. In the past, the Doctor has travelled to E-Space, but I don't recognize any of the planes of existence in this book. 
 The author did do a great job of getting the dialog right between the Doctor and Amy.

ThunderStruck is my first book by Kendall Grace and it certainly won't be my last. I fell in love with this book and these characters from the very beginning. 
 Jo Montgomery has decided the best way to get away from her public life and potentially public divorce was to move away to a small town in Georgia and just leave it all behind. Buying a house listed as a "fixer upper" sight unseen seemed risky, but she didn't care. However, being face to face with this hasty decision was a different matter altogether. Wow, this was going to take a lot of work, a lot of professional help and Jo had no idea where to even start. Just about ready to admit defeat, Jo looks up and sees the sexiest man she's ever seen standing in her doorway. Flustered, Jo learns that he is her nearest neighbor and a nice guy. He tells her to come to his place tomorrow and he can give her a list of handy men that can help her out with the place. The thought of seeing him the next day makes her feel things she's only read about in books. 
 Hawk Stephens is half Apache and believes very much in signs. One look at Jo and he knows that she was sent for him. All the signs are there and she makes him feel things he's never felt before. Being around her for a short time he learns quickly that Jo is as skittish as the horses he trains. Something in Jo's past has her scared and he knows he has to take things slow, so he doesn't scare her away. That's easier said than done when all he can think of doing is stripping her naked and having his way with her. 
 "You're killing me over here. But damn if you're not worth it." 
 This book is hot! I absolutely loved Hawk and his beliefs. When things got tough he questioned this faith a few times, but he fought on. The supporting characters in this book were a joy. Hawk's father made me laugh out loud a lot! I loved that he and Jo became a team. Even though he loved his son, he had room for a friendship with Jo and it was the sweetest thing to read. 
 I would like to thank NetGalley.com for the loan of this book in exchange for my honest review. 
 You can find this review and others at http://riverinaromantics.blogspot.com and http://tinar1121.blogspot.com

Actual rating is a 3.5. 
 Jennifer L. Armentrout will always be my favorite author, but this book just doesn't compare to her other books. I was definitely hooked on reading it, but some scenes were rushed, unnecessary, or cheesy. Would recommend to everyone, but definitely read her other books first!

I'm pretty shocked by how much I enjoyed this. I should probably be ashamed too, but I'm not! I was so pleasantly surprised by this. Big Teen Novels (BTNs) are usually so vapid and disappointing (see: Twilight and Beautiful Creatures), and while this is no means a deep book, it is much smarter than other BTNs and had less filler. I liked that Clary was strong and stepped up to the fight, even though she's completely out of her element, instead of just letting Jace take care of everything. I liked that the twists actually felt surprising, and turned everything on its head. I hadn't thought that the urban fantasy setting would appeal to me, but I liked reading about a grittier world than I normally do. Everything felt more dangerous than in other teen fantasy books, and that definitely appeals to girls that like bad boy heroes. Of course, Jace is immensely charming, snarky, and crushable, although I don't think I should think that since I'm not a teen. Don't judge me.

Until around the last 2 chapters I was happy. I was expecting a wonderful happy ending after everything was over. Instead, I got just a so-so ending. Not what I wanted, but better than a sad one. 
 I love George again, but I still don't see why he hides everything from Katerina. If he really wanted to die, she'd let him. Neither of them really seems to understand each other. I wish that the end would have been a peak into the future with George healthy again or with their new family. I don't like the way it ends with George's future being uncertain and not in a good way. 
 However, I liked the change in Danilo. It was hard to let myself like him, but in comparison to Konstantin, he was an angel. I also was glad that everyone seemed to appreciate Katerina's gift and accept her into the imperial family.

It was totally sweet meeting Kane and Avery. They are truly a matchmaking couple and you feel their love on every page. 
 The end made me cry so hard, really I was so emotionally involved... 
 At the end Kindle Alexander gave the reader a bit relieve. 
 Again a great book by Kindle Alexander. :)
Such a good book. Atticus Finch is my new hero.

The suspense was as tight as the first book and it was gratifying to see that our heroine's moral compass remained true. There was only one possible outcome for this book and we all knew where the video clip was hidden, but the manner in which things went down, the way she managed to get hold of the clip, the revelations and tightly knotted strings of coincidence were all wonderful surprises that me eager to turn the page and find out where exactly Ms Ahern was going with each new angle.. 
 It was a fairly slow start, like a train pulling out of a station, but it built and built, with a few sections where the action seemed to pause momentarily before, whoosh!, we were off again, revisiting previous adversaries and making new friends. Just when you thought all hope was lost, she managed to pull another rabbit out her hat of tricks. 
 If you are put off by other people's comments of a love triangle, don't be as there isn't one. Our heroine is let down constantly by people she thought she could trust usually because they are undergoing their own crisis of conscience at the same as she needs support; in Art's case his crisis is further strangled by the tether of filial loyalty. 
 The end felt a little harried, particularly the scene in the courtyard, but I suppose it was in keeping with the nature of the action that occurred. 
 I received this book from NetGalley for review purposes.

SO GREAT: 
 An entire book in which the Main Character does not once mention her own beauty! 
 MC actually has common sense for once. 
 No love triangles! 
 Actual talent, training, and explanations for specific skill sets. Our hero isn't perfect! 
 Hallelujah! 
 Seriously, readers: I enjoyed this. Essie is exactly as kickass as she appears, and we see evidence of it because she develops her talents throughout the book. Stitching Snow deserves way more positive press. Pass it on!

When a homicide of a local teenager occurs, District Attorney Andy Barber is assigned to the case. As the investigation into the murder deepens, it appears that Barber is too close to the crime and is officially removed as DA just as his son is revealed to be the prime suspect. Barber's world is turned upside down as he does everything in his power to prove his son's innocence. As further suspicions, doubts and motives surface, Barber stops at nothing. 
 The rather unlikable character of Andy Barber, and his son for that matter, made me dislike the book on the whole. Andy's patronizing nature towards his wife and the distant 'its-not-my-area' parenting-style were countered with a sudden, overly protective interest in his son. It all felt stilted and disingenuous. But perhaps this was the result of the audiobook narration. Barber sounded standoffish, to the point of passive-aggressive, especially in those agonizing therapy sessions with his wife. 
 Despite the heavy legal proceedings and interwoven timelines, Landay kept me intrigued. And then he blindsided me with the ending twist.

Okay. This 200-paged prequel is absolutely genius. It was SO GOOD. Like beyond words for good. 
 I chose to read this because I just cannot wait for Dorothy Must Die, and what's better than beginning with a prequel to start you onto the story? Let me tell you, nothing is better than that. 
 I've always loved the story of The Wizard of Oz. There is such an amazing story behind the story (bear with me, this will make sense) and I got everything I asked for. By the end of the prequel, (I keep wanting to say novel,) all of my questions about the mysterious Dorothy Gale were answered, and I instantly realized what type of person she came to be. 
 These days, I find that retellings end up so bad. But this one absolutely was amazing. Danielle Paige received such a smart idea to her head. We all know Dorothy Gale as an innocent, quiet country girl, but this story goes the whole other way, and what happened after the main story. 
 So this book focuses on the main story, which is great. We don't have to plot a whole new beginning into our minds, and we don't have to start over fresh with a whole new protagonist. If you have the main idea of who Dorothy Gale is and what previously has happened to her, then you got the right idea and this series will be for you. 
 So Dorothy went totally crazy in this prequel, but not in a bad way. Everything was much more detailed, and we saw her true personality. 
 Is it just me, or was Glenda the real villain in this book? Everything basically happened because of her, and in the end, when she did that whole motherly-love act, I JUST REALIZED THAT IT'S ALL BECAUSE OF HER. I felt as if I got hit with a bunch of bricks in the head. Ozma was absolutely adorable and kick-ass, by the way. :) Villain=love 
 Magic really is stupid. I just realized that in this book. It just changed Dorothy completely, and it made me hate her so much. She acted LIKE SHE WAS TAKING OVER THE PLACE AND SHE WAS RULING ALL OF OZ. This cannot be. >:( Okay, I lied. Maybe I still have one question. What next? Does magic still overtake Dorothy and make her a bitch? Well, this was a prequel, so I guess we'll find out in the real deal, but seriously, I treated this like a full-length book, and I was absolutely stunned by its amazingness. Dorothy, seriously, must die. *slams keyboard*

Second read, July 2015 
 First read, May 2013

"I do not know why you two are circling each other like stars. It is not my cosmic dance. But I do know that you come asking after one another, when only a few strides and a handful of stairs divide you." 
 It took me some time to write this review, because I didn't know how to put the quality of this book into words. I don't know how Schwab does it each time, but I do know she has magic working at her fingertips. 
 A Gathering of Shadows was everything you could ask for in a sequel. The author's talent is undeniable, her writing polished as never before. She truly outdid herself. Her characters shine in the glittery backdrop of Red London, magic entangles everyone and no one is immune to its consequences. 
 The Characters. 
 Lila. The way I see it, this was Lila's book. True, we get to see a lot of Kell too, but Lila takes the spotlight for the better part of the novel, in my opinion. She is reckless and dangerous. Her actions are brash, and even if she is talented, she doesn't know when to stop. I've read other reviews that slightly complained about this - which I can definitely see. I think the author wanted to portray a character that was pushed to the brink by years of solitude, and the will to escape. 
 Kell. A kind-hearted magician. His character is always the steadiest one, the one that keeps others safe. I truly felt sad for him, but this book allows him to go through a journey of growth that he needed. Save him Lila, please!  
 Alucard and Rhy are definitely the most fascinating pair, and they work magnificently. Honestly, Alucard is pure gold and Rhy, oh well, no words needed. 
 All in all, everything about this book shimmered with magic. Firstly, it contained a Magic Tournament. Yes, you heard me right. Then, it contained shadows coming to life. Quite literally. Then, it had undiscovered magic talents. Antari mysteries. Worlds coming back to life. Magic coming back to worlds. 
 In other words, pick this book up. It won't disappoint.

I'm on a book-high. You know when you finish a really good book? And afterwards you're completely filled with happiness and no thoughts besides the good book? That's me. 
 I'm filled. Overflowing with happiness. Happiness is pouring from me.Seriously.. . I can't contain myself. 
 But there's also sadness because how long will I have to wait to find another book that can do that to me? How long will I have to wait for a YA romance to truly move me? The last YA romance that read that did that was Rainbow Rowell's fangirl. 
 You know? It will be a while before I find another gem like this one. 
 And here's a secret: Stephanie Perkins' books are my to-go books whenever I get sad. I've read "Anna & The French Kiss" & "Lola & The Boy Next Door" over a dozen times. Their pages are filled with highlighted sections, exclamation marks, hearts and sad faces. My very first copy of Anna is so worn out, so written on, that I had to buy another. That's how much I love these novels. 
 Of course the road of how we got to Isla wasn't a easy one. I'll be honest to say I was a bit put off when it was pushed farther away from it's original publication. Perkins then spoke about her struggle with depression and I was so shocked. She's written these books that are my cure for my waves of depression. I could understand how terrified she must of been of writing a book when her other books have garnered such high ratings. I get it. And I love her because she didn't give up. If I were her I probably would have. But she didn't. She fought through it and she gave us what will definitely be one of the best books of 2014. 
 And I would wait twenty more years if I knew that Isla was going to be this good. So I went looking for Isla last Friday because rumors were that some Barnes & Nobles had released her a week early. (I still preordered her! Because they are giving them signed AND WITH BUTTONS) I found her and I rushed home to devour her. And let me tell you. It. Was. Amazing!!! 
 IDEK HOW TO FEEEEL! 
 Let's start with the beginning: the first 5 chapters were released a while ago: 
 (Here's the link: http://issuu.com/penguinteen/docs/isl... ) 
 Having read that a million times! (I'm not even joking) I knew I would have a special connection with Isla. I loved her dorkiness. I loved her self-consciousness. She felt real. Isla. . . 
 I don't want to spoil anything but I will say this: 
 As the story progresses we get a lot of emotions. I was so jittery and happy. I LOVE Isla's feminine side! She's very girlie and I LOVE TAHT! Nowadays, I feel like YA heroines are "one of the guys and she wears sneakers and no make up. She's a t-shirt kind of girl". It is such bullshit. I'm fucking girlie as hell and I'm also able to hang out with guys and not fall into the stereotypical role. I have colorful hair and wear dresses (I even it out with some doc martens;)) but Isla is feminine and she wears scary heels and she decorates very girlie and I LOVE IT! I love her. 
 Then there's Josh. And oh lord I can only try to not give anything away but there's so much more to Josh. I ADORE ST. CLAIR but Josh? He's beyond St. Clair. (IDEK HOW THATS POSSIBLE!!) AND I LOVEEEE ST CLAIR. so how can I say that? 
 Okay, round up: I laughed A LOT. I cried. I got frustrated. I felt everything Isla felt. I felt for Josh. I was overloaded with emotion! Jesus. I-I-I can't. It's perfect. 
 Oh and if your wondering how much the gang from "Anna" or "Lola" come out? It's not much. They make a brief appearance towards the end BUT WHEN THEY DO WHOLY CHEESE BALLS IWASSOHAPPYILOVEDITSOMUCH!!! 
 That's it. Read this book. That huge gap we got from Lola to Isla only made everything bittersweet. It was perfect. Thank you Stephanie<3 THANK YOUU! ILOVEYOUSOMUCH.

The blurb says " 
 Acclaimed bestselling novelist Kunihiko Hidaka is found brutally murdered in his home on the night before he's planning to leave Japan and relocate to Vancouver. His body is found in his office, a locked room, within his locked house, by his wife and his best friend, both of whom have rock solid alibis. Or so it seems. At the crime scene, Police Detective Kyochiro Kaga recognizes Hidaka's best friend, Osamu Nonoguchi. Years ago when they were both teachers, they were colleagues at the same public school. Kaga went on to join the police force while Nonoguchi eventually left to become a full-time writer, though with not nearly the success of his friend Hidaka. As Kaga investigates, he eventually uncovers evidence that indicates that the two writers' relationship was very different that they claimed, that they were anything but best friends. But the question before Kaga isn't necessarily who, or how, but why. In a brilliantly realized tale of cat and mouse, the detective and the killer battle over the truth of the past and how events that led to the murder really unfolded. And if Kaga isn't able to uncover and prove why the murder was committed, then the truth may never come out. 
 " 
 This book begins with typical Keigo Higashino style with a quick reveal of who the murderer is. The rest of the book is all about the detective trying to find out the motive of the said crime. The novel has a epistolary style which is rarely used in detective fiction. This particularly suits this book, as one is immediately sucked into each character's version of events. 
 What I do find irritating  is the completely bullshit motive that is revealed at the end. This ending is right there with the likes of Old Boy, Vol. 1 manga series. For one, there is no way any detective in the police is going to unearth stuff by going to such extremes as investigating an incident during their childhood when a confession has already been made. I am sorry real world policemen are too busy to get so deeply enmeshed in a case. Secondly, for a book about motive, the motive is utter crap. There is literally no reason to do any such thing as murder for the flimsy reason given in the book.  
 Overall, I would recommend other works by this author such as The Devotion of Suspect X & Salvation of a Saint before reading this one.

I wasn't entirely sure what I'd think of the book when I started it- the fact that it was in first person being the first mark against it. But the time period is one I've been fascinated with for years. (Well, to be precise, I've been fascinated with Cesare Borgia, which means my area of interest is about a century earlier, but close enough. And imagining the hero as a light-haired Cesare Borgia, Assassin's Creed style, certainly didn't hurt.) 
 But somehow the first person worked for me in this book. Usually I hate not knowing what the hero's thinking, but in this case the narration gave enough information about him that I could generally get a sense of it, even if the heroine thought he was thinking something different. 
 Can I say I find heroes like this adorable? I don't know, somehow that seems kind of (very) strange, but I do. I think part of it was his childishness, but somehow, despite how much of a creep he was, he still managed to seem adorable to me. (Even if he was a rapist who tortured and executed people for no reason.) 
 I will say that I didn't quite get why the heroine fell in love with the hero as early in the book as she did. Up to that point, he certainly hadn't exactly acted all that nicely to her. 
 The second half of the book also dragged a bit. I just wanted to yell at them to stop being so proud and just talk to each other about their feelings already! 
 But I definitely enjoyed the book, certainly more than expected. (And I wish there were more romances set in Renaissance Italy.)

I actually didn't see the trigger warning (I'm not disappointed that I didn't, because I can be triggered by this stuff and I might've skipped it and this is a book that's not to be missed) but therefore I honestly wasn't expecting any of this when I started reading the book, which just made it so much better. I honestly didn't understand the preface at all until I was halfway through the book and finally understood what was going on. 
 This book was really well written, it obviously came from the heart (with a dash of writing talent thrown in). But it was also triggering as fuck. Just a fair warning. 
 I will admit, I shed a few tears reading this book.  Like when I was reading everything that was going through James's mind; all his turmoil and I could just feel how much he blamed himself and how he just couldn't go on anymore. I also was in tears when a chapter ended with his suicice attempt and the next one began by a grave - I honestly thought that he was dead.  
 I'm fairly happy with the ending, normally I like sad endings where the main character dies, but this was so much better. His struggles were so real and I could feel his pain. I think this was also a great book to read for those who don't understand the inner workings of mental illnesses. The author executed it perfectly - James's thoughts were spot-on and I really got him. I was kind of sad that there wasn't a magical cure for it, only because it's most likely true, there isn't a cure for a mental illness like this one and that just tears me down because I can't face that. I don't know if that was a good thing or a bad thing - but since it was realistic, I'm gonna go with good.  
 I loved everything about this book. The characters were all so realistic and well done, especially James's mum. She wasn't that typical literature bitch - she was just a real life mum that didn't understand mental illnesses and acted in the only way she knew how to act.  Another character that was great was Jess - I genuinely liked her and I thought that she was a great friend. I also found Mike an intriguing character, I felt that he was most likely projecting his own disappointment with not being higher up in the company by being a rude pretentious asshole that clearly didn't value his staff. 
 I also loved Theo and James's relationship - especially their playlists. 
 All in all: An incredibly moving story that leaves you in tears but also with a heart filled with hope Trigger warning: self-harm (cutting and burning), scars, suicide attempt, bipolar disorder, depression, overdose, mania  
 4.9 stars, -0.1 because nothing's perfect

I read Lemony Snicket books in between taking care of my son. He has moments when he is both needy AND stubborn and I have to wait him out, and so in those moments I read. I usually choose a short book and can finish it in oh, a week or so. 
 Here's this one... 
  
 It's one more horrible adventure with the long-suffering Baudelaire children. OMG, and just when I thought nothing could be worse than Books 1, 2, and 3 - was I wrong! At least in those books the three kids - Violet, 14; Klause, 12; Sunny, a baby - get a little respite at the beginning of each book. Their new guardian will treat them kindly - if weirdly - in the first chapter or so. They get a nice bed or decent food or a huge library to wander around in, but NOT in The Miserable Mill! In this book, the new guardian forces them - immediately! - to work in a lumber mill where they peel bark off logs, use saws to make planks, then bind the logs in string and stamp them. They get ONE meal a day and live in a dormitory with lots of oppressed and pathetic workers. I hated this! I mean, give them a break, come on, Lemony! Okay, there IS a library but it contains three boring books, and even poor little Sunny is forced to work in the lumber mill... 
 Plus the one kind-of-nice person, Charles, is a wimp! And an idiot. And utterly useless. As is Mr. Poe, who manages their fortune and tries to keep it from their evil Uncle Olaf. And you just know at some point the kids will run into Olaf somewhere, somehow and they do. 
 Of course, eventually, the kids' intelligence, creativity and internal will to get-through-just-about-anything will prevail, but this time with a twist: Violet, who's the inventor, has to read to figure out how to get out of this dire predicament; and Klaus, who's the reader/researcher, has to turn inventor to do the same. I sometimes think Sunny with her biting teeth and infant dialogue, is my fav. character. :D 
  
 There's also the fact that Lemony continually uses 'big words' or unusual ones, or ones that children don't necessarily know, so of course, you're gonna 'learn as you read.' Generally speaking, this is not my kind of book. I mean I hate it when a book is all about 'teaching something,' and I am a former teacher who dealt with 'big words' all the time. (And don't get me going on preachy books either.) So this is my least fav. part of old Lemony... 
 But the book's a good one, and not because of the story, which has its lame parts, as in its use of hypnotism. The book is good due to the indefatigable - there's a word for you, Lemony - spirit of the three Baudelaire children. I'll keep reading the series... 
 Four stars.

This book was a mind trip of the best kind! 
 First Line: 
 So, the thing is, I come from the world we were suppose to have, p.1. 
 The entire world is annihilated because of a woman. Okay, that's too simplistic. Tom Barren lives in the year 2016, but instead of a world like the one we live in, his world is full of technological wonders we're still dreaming of. Teleportation, flying cars, and yes, even time travel. Okay, that's a bit of an exaggeration. Time travel is currently being developed in Tom Barren's world and will soon be available for consumption on a mass scale. Time travel tourism! But that never happens, because even though this is the future and it's full of all kinds of high tech advancements, Tom is an impulsive idiot. And because of him and a woman named Penelope, who really doesn't give two cents about him, the world of tomorrow is destroyed and all we're left with is our today. Okay, okay, that's not quite it either, but it's closer. I highly recommend just reading the book. 
 When you live in a world of universal plenty, people genuinely aspire to make things that work well. They didn't want to trick their customers. They wanted to help them be happier. Whereas it turns out my specialty is disappointment and ruin, p. 58. 
 What Dazzled: Omg, I'm still thinking about this book! There's so many wonderful paragraphs, pages, and chapters about harnessing energy and how to actually time travel and what would be the consequences of time travel and it's so much fun to sit and think about and compare it to other sci-fi novels' theories and actual science. I'm such a nerd! Then there's the short chapters that make it so easy to read a little bit here and a little there, but also short enough to entice you to read just a couple more chapters. This is also one of those books that when you get done reading it you want to immediately reread it, so you can see all the twists coming at you. 
 What Fizzled: At first I really disliked the character Tom Barren. Gawd he's is such a whiny loser. But stick with it, because he's a lot more interesting than just a whiny loser. 
 Jots and Thoughts: Is Elan Mastai a secret scientist who really has discovered how to time travel? I'm just curious. He is for sure a Canadian screenwriter whose movies are What If, Alone in the Dark, and The Samaritan.

I thoroughly enjoyed Suarez's previous two books so I wasn't surprised to enjoy this one, too. I was a bit disappointed that he employed some of the typical technothriller cliches of the hot smart science chick falling for the brutally handsome warrior, but the rest of it plays so well and crackles with so much energy that I'm going to forgive him those sins. 
 What I can't quite get over, however, is the fact that this is basically just an update of Dean Ing's 1993 technothriller Butcher Bird. They both concern drones attacking Middle East targets who then go up against a special ops group working "off the reservation" to combat this new techno-terror. However, just as Justin Cronin's The Passage is a superior remake to Stephen King's The Stand, Kill Decision is a superior remake of Ing's book. Where Ing was actually a bit more prescient and ahead of the curve, Suarez really makes this feel as if this could be possible tomorrow. Suarez's version is also not as ham-fisted as Ing's was: the finale of Kill Decision feels organic to what we've already been introduced to whereas the ending to Butcher Bird really had some deus ex machina to it (especially how the explosion of a nuclear powerpack conveniently hit the hero with the exact amount of radiation to cure his brain tumor). 
 I really liked the information about weaver ants and how it was being used as a basis for automated systems. This feels like a plausible alternative to the way Skynet might operate in the Terminator universe. Instead of top-down control by a killer supercomputer, Suarez postulates a simple insect hive-mind behavior that is even more deadly. The cover with its robotic ants nicely ties into that. 
 I feel like I learned a couple cool little things from this book and had a cracking good time doing so.

 Some kudos to the girl is that she knows what she wants to find out and is pretty determined to get her answers-despite the consequences it could have on her (and everyone else), though this recklessness could simply be due to her feeling she has no options in life and wanting to escape the world she is caged in. She showed how people got angry, selfish and didn't think about anything other than what's going on right there right then. 3.5-3.75 stars 
 Mercy Wong has finished her education at the Oriental Public School in San Francisco, the one school she and her fellow Chinese-American youth are allowed to attend. Mercy has big dreams, however, and a plan to lift her family out of poverty. She plans to become an herbal tea merchant and marry her best friend Tom, who is supposed to succeed his father as a Chinese medicine doctor. She especially wants to ensure her frail younger brother doesn't have to take over their Ba's laundry business. Armed with her bible, The Book for Business-Minded Women by a Mrs. Evelyn Lowry, Mercy sets out to launch her grand plan. The first step is to get in to St. Clare's, a respected girls' school on par with the Wilkes school for boys. Mercy knows it will be difficult to convince the board to allow her in because of her race and her family's economic situation, but Mercy has a few tricks up her sleeve. Upon starting at the school, Mercy must pretend to be a Chinese heiress, deal with a mean girl, avoid a caning from Headmistress and practice comportment. St. Clare's is not an academic school but a finishing school. Even though it's not what Mercy expected, she's determined to succeed at any cost. When tragedy strikes on April 18, 1906, Mercy's world is upended. It would be easy to give in to despair like everyone else she knows, but that's not Mercy's way. She uses her very un-ladylike, un-Chinese "bossy cheeks" to find a way to save herself and her friends. 
 This is a pretty good book for young adults. I liked the multi-culturalism in the novel and learning something about Chinese-American life in the early 20th century. I was hoping for a link to Samantha from Under the Painted Sky, to discover if she made it to San Francisco and had descendants. This is a stand-alone novel though. The plot is interesting and it did really capture my attention at times. I knew about the earthquake and have read other novels about it but by the time the earthquake happens in this story, I was invested in Mercy's story and needed to know what happened. What does happen is a bit surprising and very interesting though not exactly realistic. I wasn't thrilled with the homage to A Little Princess. That was unnecessary and been done too many times as was Melody's struggle with Elodie. My biggest quibble was that Francesca wouldn't use the word pasta but macaroni. I'm not sure if there was a sizable enough Italian population in San Francisco in 1906 to even warrant an Italian restaurant. The food would be foreign and unfamiliar to anyone else. [OK apparently there were 15,000 of them in San Francisco alone... thanks Google]. I also wasn't completely thrilled with the little bit of preachiness at the end. There's a slight religious element to the book: Mercy's Ba is Christian, Ma practices a blend of Eastern religions and St. Clare's is a Catholic school. 
 I loved Mercy and her "bossy cheeks." Sometimes I thought she was crazy but she is 15 and I remember being very silly at that age. Rules were meant to be tested at that age. Mercy is caring and compassionate when it comes to her family. She's a bit tough to befriend though because she's so brazen, devil-may-care. I liked how much she loved her family and how all she did was for them. She was the best big sister. Her relationship with Tom felt a little forced. I liked how she never gives up and finds a way to accomplish her goals. 
 My favorite secondary character was Francesca, an Italian girl who loves to feed people. That's kind of the norm for Italians though. Francesca's family's restaraunt. It doesn't make Francesca unique. I quibble a bit at her attending a white, exclusive girls' school. Italian girls were expected to help their mothers and take care of their parents. I am not sure she would be engaged already in her teens. Marcus is a complete donkey's behind and I can't imagine her parents would want her to marry him if they knew what he was like. Headmistress won't let that happen! 
 Mercy's other school friends are difficult to distinguish. They each have distinct personalities and backgrounds but I kept getting confused as to which was which. An audiobook with a full cast or different voices would help with this confusion, especially since there are a lot of characters in this book. I liked the girls, especially the Texan. Elodie is a typical mean girl with the typical story. She gets more unique and interesting after the earthquake. The same is true for Headmistress. 
 I wasn't thrilled with Tom. I could have done without the romance. It didn't really add anything to the story. I admire Tom for his ambition and going for his dream, but the way he did it was not great. He's absent for most of the book so the relationship feels tacked on afterwards. He serves to give Mercy a dream and someone else to care about. 
 The most vibrant minor characters are Mercy's family. I liked them a lot. They're very colorful and interesting. Her mother is a bit too dramatic with her fortune telling business, and doom and gloom predictions. Ba is sometimes hard on Mercy but he loves her and teaches her to be the young woman she is. Mercy's little brother, Jack, is very sweet. 
 I liked this book with it's tough main character. It's not quite as compelling as Under the Painted Sky but parts are interesting and I was eager to find out what happened to Mercy next. I especially liked the feeling towards the end when The girls start Mercy's Kitchen and feed 100+ people. The coming together the author described in her note sounded like the feeling after 9/11. The outcome after rebuilding is the same too.  
 Content warning spoiler : 
 Mild language. Mercy refers to a specific root as looking like a "man's energy pouch. Also 
 There's rumors the priest has a girlfriend and when searching for him after the earthquake, Mercy finds him in dead in bed, naked, with a married woman. Elodie's father has a mistress.
One thing to say about this book: It could have been so much more.
And what, I wonder, was the deal with all those little gold treasures hidden in the shelf?

Credit where credit is due: this was an incredible audiobook. The reading was done skillfully and beautifully by Carmen Rose, who tackled the Scottish brogue and necessary Gaelic very well, considering that she had to spend 50% of the time voicing a variety of male Scottish highlanders, and the other 50% of the time voicing a painfully timid and insipid English miss. This raises the crucial problem of the book: the timid and insipid English miss. I get it, people are shy, people have serious mental and emotional hangups of all shapes and sizes, but this heroine was too much of a shrinking violet for me to enjoy her story, even after the root cause was explained. The plot problems that this emotional flaw caused and resolved were critical to the story, and I have no real ideas about how else the author could have resolved them, but the excruciating freezing shyness made me fail to connect with the lady, which I find to be an important element in true and deep enjoyment of a romance. If you're into Diana Gabaldon at all, this will likely work for you, even though Maddie is no Claire. Captain MacKenzie was verra verra fun, and draws heavily on the tropes that made Jamie Fraser such a popular hunk, but without the bum trauma and being a wanted man and beating his wife and all that. The glacier-like pace of physical intimacy between them led to some very hot and spicy scenes, but the absurd level of reserve from Madeleine and the rather over-the-top showers of loving endearments (excessive mush!) at the conclusion held me back from a higher rating. I liked quite a bit of the writing, including Ms. Dare's clever trick of always providing an absurd pet whose situation mirrors that of the lovers central to the story (in this case, the lobsters), and adding in a few repeating tropes that become inside jokes, a private language understood only by the lovers and their voyeuristic readers. I also appreciated the attempt to teach historical elements about the return of Scotsmen from war. Not a perfect book, but a jolly fun romp, and a good listen.

Whenever my sister recommends a book to me that features a love triangle, she always tells me which guy I should root for (i.e., which guy is her favourite). When my sister told me to read this series, she said, "You like Warner." 
 After finishing the first book, I thought she was crazy. Warner was horrible. Terrible. Besides that, I found the first book kind of dull in many ways. Particularly, I found Juliette and Adam boring. 
 If you have read the first book, and are having similar feelings, stick with it. Because my issues mostly went away in the second book, and were all but completely non-existent by the end of the third. 
 First of all, Juliette goes through a lot of character development over the course of the three novels, and she is almost unrecognizable in the third book compared to how she was in the first. She admits this, too, how much she has changed. So if she seems meek in the first book, it's because she is. But as she becomes more aware of her powers and how to control them, she becomes stronger in so many ways. 
 This book also explains a lot of Warner's more morally questionable actions in the third book. It still doesn't make him a good guy, but he doesn't pretend to be one, either. We also learn more details about him that make him more sympathetic. However, he never, ever answers for what he did to Adam in the first book. Never. I would have liked him to, especially given that Warner finds out Adam is his brother, finally . I do like that we get to learn the meaning behind his IGNITE tattoo ("I Give Nothing. I Take Everything." ). 
 If I have one complaint, and I do, it's that the entire novel was building up to this epic war, this final confrontation with Anderson, and it only lasted a few pages. There's also a lot left up in the air in terms of the future of the world. I don't have a lot of faith in Juliette as the leader of the nation. But I guess we'll never know.  
 Still, I really liked this book, probably my favourite in the trilogy. The scenes between Warner and Juliette are hot. I'm glad Mafi didn't shy away from putting sexy scenes in a YA novel. 
 Also, her writing is beautiful. I have said it so many times in my reviews of this series, but it cannot be said enough. I'm looking forward to reading anything else she writes in the future, because I cannot get enough of her gorgeous prose.

 Update January 2017: I feel an overwhelming urge to read the sequel, for reasons I can't really pin down. Maybe it's because I so so so badly wanted and expected to love the first one, and didn't, that I just don't feel fulfilled? This was supposed to be my favourite book, I just felt that very strongly and I can't explain why. I keep coming back to this review to tweak it and I'm not sure why I do that either. I think I read it wrong, I don't know. I just feel disappointed, but it's not like the author ever owed me anything. I even got rid of the book then re-purchased it at a used bookstore despite how angry it made me. I can't explain. It's the one that got away or something. 
 Gabaldon's writing is absolutely beautiful and engaging, though I didn't enjoy much else about Outlander. Her descriptions of the time period and the castles satisfied my curiosity enough, and it was easy to picture all of the locations. The accents were easy to read and not annoying which was appreciated. I was surprised at how much reviewers mention the sex in this book though, either gushingly or negatively, as it glosses over it nearly every time. I didn't find I really cared in the end either way, as there was enough else going on, I just wasn't expecting that from all of the talk. 
 The reason I couldn't love this as much as I desperately wanted to was because I didn't love the characters. That's not to say I strongly disliked either of them, I just wasn't enamored. Part of this could have been because I had spoilers regarding some of Jamie's actions, so I couldn't grow to love him as other readers did, knowing all of the bad things to come. I had a hard time with Claire's acceptance of a lot of these things/events, even if she was momentarily not okay with them, as she got over it really quickly.  I'm talking about that part where he beat her, then she was mad for a minute, then told him she UNDERSTOOD, and then he proceeded to joke about it throughout the rest of the novel . I also couldn't understand Jamie's back and forth between being a controlling, possessive freak and a naive, somewhat childish boy. Yes, everyone has 3-dimensional personalities in real life and you can be strong and childish, but the way he was written was simply inconsistent and contradictory. 
 I found there were a lot of random events and minor plot points thrown in just for the sake of making Claire look useful- like the birthing of the foal. Jamie would have done just fine; his hands would not have been "too big" to reach inside the mare's birthing canal. A baby horse has to fit out of there! I felt like this happened a lot, where weird excuses were made to put characters in certain situations. Some of these situations didn't even feed the overall plot or were just so unlikely that they made me want to roll my eyes. I think Gabaldon went overkill on her research and felt compelled to include every single bit of old Scottish lore, geography, and miscellaneous information on botany, horses and witchcraft, just because she could. Parts just felt like a history lesson. 
 I intended to read the sequel, but the last 100 pages of this were dryer than anything, so I'm undecided at the moment. 
 Overall it was worth the read, despite it feeling like a chore, and the writing style and voice served it well. The characters had their moments where I could enjoy them as people, and a few of the little tangents were fascinating despite derailing the plot. I've never read anything about Scotland and I appreciate the taste of it Gabaldon gave me.

 I can't say too much more without giving it away -- if you enjoy fairytale retellings, definitely give this one a shot. I rated it a 5/5 on Goodreads and added it to my favorites shelf.

Another example of a book I would have liked when I was in high school/younger but doesn't really fit me anymore. 
 Of course, I always wish my life was a book. I'd be living it up as a Slytherin in Hogwarts if that was the case. But Phoebe Martin, our bookish protagonist, takes it to a whole new level, and tries to change her personality to match that of her favorite heroines in order to impress the guy she likes. 
 The story in general was rambly and didn't really have a definite direction, so you don't really get to the point until halfway through the book. It was mostly day to day typical school adventures of Phoebe and her friends, along with her love of knitting and books. There was also the stereotypical crush on popular guy turns into crush on guy that's so much better for her.

I've heard people rave about how Doc Smith's work was one of the early space operas and that it influenced many later science fiction masterpieces. This may be true, but I'm thinking that just because it was influential, doesn't mean I have to like it. And I don't much. 
 It's been pointed out by others that this book hasn't aged well, and maybe that's my problem with it. Then again, the Hardy Boys haven't aged well, and I still (guilty pleasure alert) like some of the series. But I read those as a child, so there's a bit of nostalgia that goes with my reading of the Hardy Boys. Not so with Smith's novel, Triplanetary. I wasn't a child when Doc Smith's first works came out, so I don't have that glittering/blinding cloud of nostalgia around his work, like the one that engulfs me when I read Hardy Boys. 
 Maybe seeing Flash Gordon reruns at about the same time that Star Wars came out back in the '70s caused a rift in my mind, a gaping gulf between "then" and "now" (or what was "now" at the time). Pan Star Wars all you want, but the original movie is both derived from the old Flash Gordon serials and a reworking of the trappings in a beautiful and brilliant "new" (again, speaking relatively of time) packaging. I loved it, and still do. Flash Gordon is laughable, and was laughable even when I was a child. And because it's laughable, I kind of enjoy the campiness of it all. But I don't take it as seriously as it takes itself. 
 And maybe that's my problem. Perhaps I went into this book ready to take it seriously, hence I was seriously disappointed. I can't look back on it and glory in the unintentional silliness of it all - the chauvinism, the absolutely terrible dialogue, and the deus ex machina (and here, I mean literally "machine") that jerks the plot in unlikely directions and destroys pacing. All of this makes for an agitating read full of overstimulus, like overdosing on cocaine or deciding, against all better judgement, that you should take the plunge off the 3 story tall water slide only to find that it wasn't such a good idea just as your butt clears the drop. Smith's attempts in this vein seem like a way to buy off, rather than reward the reader for patience. And I know not everyone wrote like that back in that day and age, so don't feed me the "His writing was a product of the time" line. 
 The one aspect of the book that I did enjoy didn't involve the human characters at all. I actually quite liked the alien race, the Nevians. But the whole mess between Triplanetary (the human alliance) and these amphibian aliens could have been avoided, had someone just stopped for a moment and talked about the abundance of iron resources available in the asteroid belt. Why didn't anyone think of that? Can't we all just get along?!? 
 So I finished the book. I can honestly say that. I won't be reading any more of E.E. "Doc" Smith's work, however. I've had enough. Too much, in fact. I can only be force-fed so many unlikely twists and perfect saves before declaring: "Doc Smith is to hyperbole in science fiction what Monty Hall was to giveaways." 
 Still, I liked the aliens. At least they made sense. In fact, rather than destroying the galaxy, the aliens are saving a bit of the galaxy by keeping my rating of this book at two stars, rather than one.

I can't even explain how excited I was to find this book. I love PNR and I really love historical romance. I was so sure this book was going straight to my favorites list. Not so much. 
 I love the concept. Vampires that exist peacefully and secretly among the ton. There are Lords of different cities in England (and other countries as well, I'm sure), all part of a vampire hierarchy. There are vampire hunters as well. These are all good things, they were just executed terribly. 
 The conflict is centered around Dr. Polidori and his newly published book about a vampire, sparking an interest around England in vampires. Now the actual vampires are worried about being discovered. One way for the vampire Lord of London to throw off suspicion of his vampirism is to take a mortal English bride. Plus, he wants to sleep with her. Win-win. 
 What didn't work for me was the lack of explanation of the vampire world. We learn only what Angelica asks. If she's not curious about it, we don't learn about it. And I had a lot of unanswered questions. And the flying? What? How high does he fly? How does that work? Why the hell wasn't Angelica freaked out? It's not like she's used to being in planes. This was the first time in her life she was off the ground. It bordered on bizarre.  
 We learn that vampires also have random talents (such as flying and mind reading). Angelica was not surprised by any of them. Her responses to learning certain people had these traits basically translated into "Oh you can read my mind? Nifty! You can fly? Cool!" It was completely unbelievable. Especially for a woman in the early 19th century. 
 The romance was underwhelming. For some reason, Angelica's behavior and way of speaking reminded me of Alice from Alice in wonderland. She found wondering in everyhing little thing. Everything was fascinating. She loved defying expectation just for shit and giggles. She was always overly enthusiastic. She giggled a lot. Basically, she had this childlike wonder about everything, even sex. Anything childlike, even wonder, is not sexy. I would have believed she was 14 if her age was never mentioned. Which isn't that far off for 19th century England, but for this book, it just made me uncomfortable. She was incredibly immature. Her love of reading and writing books came off as an easy way to make her seem more mature so that a man that has been alive for centuries would find her more attractive than other beautiful women. Think Belle from Beauty and the Beast. Except she's 12. 
 I'm tempted to pick another from the series and try again. Sometimes the first book in a series, especially of a genre as different as this one, can take a book or two to establish itself. I think that was the most frustrating thing about this book. It had the potential to be amazing. I probably did myself a disservice going into this book with such high hopes. And if I'm honest, the first book in a romance series isn't usually my favorite. The more the characters have time to develop by appearing in each book, the more attached I get and more emotionally invested I become. I can't really recommend this book, but I'm not swearing off the whole series.
