That's how I figured from the beginning that Simon killed himself and framed the others . And I, too, figured out Jake was in on it when he said something like 'You've ruined everything.' That should bug me, how I had it all nailed down so early on, but I can't fault it.  The three major characters in The Enchanted are nameless. I normally do not have a problem with such creative decisions, but in this case I felt that the nameless nature of the characters kept me from truly caring for them or rooting for them. 
 I also felt as though the magical elements of The Enchanted were not necessary and sometimes confusing. I understand that parts of the novel are told from the viewpoint of a man who is delusional, but I do not know if his delusions needed to be so often emphasized. 
 I would recommend The Enchanted if someone were looking for a short, thought-provocative read, but I am not sure that I would say much more about it.

The premise of the book is that on her 25th birthday CC is lonely and drunk and performs a ritual in which she asks the goddess of the earth, Gaea, to bring magic into her life. The result of this is that CC switches places with Gaea's mermaid daughter, Princess Undine. She is also sent back in time to about 1014 I believe. CC is allowed to return to land as a human (in Undine's very beautiful form) but she must return to the water and transform into a mermaid every 3 days. The only way to break this cycle is to find a man, fall in love, and have him accept her completely. On land Undine is "rescued" by a handsome solicitous knight who she assumes will be the man for her. Meanwhile, she has already encountered a merman who she is drawn to, Dylan, and they enter into an erotic relationship. 
 Now in fairness this book had it's good parts. I liked the use of mythology/fairy tale that made the story seem familiar and comfortable. I liked a lot of the descriptive ideas, like the scene where she actually becomes a mermaid--very well written. The setting was fairly intriguing, all though the time travel portion of it was somewhat pointless. The romance was passable. And from what I could tell, there are some interesting plot twists thrown in to keep things fresh. 
 My issues with this book are many. The humor is at best awkward and clumsy. It's never fully committed to. The opening scene of the book has the heroine talking to herself and pathetically drinking alone. At the same time we are supposed to believe that she's a smart professional member of the United States Air Force. I guess my problem with her character and this part of the premise is that I wanted to like her, but she's inconsistently written. I think that the author either need to commit to making a humorous slightly ditzy character, or a smart well put together one. Or give us some background to justify the lack of consistency. This problem carries over into the actual story as well. Half of the time the effort is made to give good logical reasons for things, and half of the time no explanation is given at all. The other major issues is that the characters are, for the most part, flat and underdeveloped. An effort is made to show that CC has a meaningful change in her worldview and character...but thats about it, everyone else is fairly static. Overall the writing is rough. 2 stars.

 Five Touching Stars 
 And this is what it is! A truly touching read. My heartstrings were pulled on to the limit, I cried, I laughed and fell head over heels with two absolutely gorgeous characters that had me enthralled from chapter one to the very last page. Ms Williams has told their story with such sensitivity and feeling making this standalone novel a very difficult one to put down. In fact, interruptions were frowned upon and while drying my tears or chuckling to myself, funny looks were thrown my way! 
 I couldn't find fault with this read. The storyline flows constantly, it has just the right amount of witty banter and believe me, touching scenes made me want to jump into my Kindle and give them both a hug. My first one would have been for Ryan Hale. My heart went out to her. After seven years away from her hometown, she goes back to say goodbye to someone very dear to her and explain to her childhood sweetheart why she'd disappeared into thin air. She can't find the right words though. The boy she was in love with, her hero, is now a strapping young man and has no wish to listen to the girl who broke him. 
 "Where did that troubled, hot-headed boy I grew up with go?" 
 Actually, I got a tad annoyed with Grant Turner to start off with and gave him a proverbial telling off. When the opportunity arises she plucks up the courage and ooh my, what he hears provokes such an emotional response that I couldn't help but feel sorry for both of them. 
 "That was another lifetime, Ryan. Another fucking life. We've moved on, and that's behind us now. Let's leave it there, okay?" 
 Depending on what angle I looked at Ryan's reasoning, I think her decision not to tell Grant before must have been a difficult one. On the one hand, she was selflessly concerned about how it would have affected his future. On the other, he had had a right to know. Between a rock and a hard place, now she's got no choice but to divulge what she's been hiding from him. So Grant's reaction to the news didn't surprise me in the least. Knocked sideways, I felt his frustration, his hurt and his resentment. Regardless of so many years apart, he can still read her like an open book. And he wants to know what else she's keeping back from him. 
 "You were the one person in the world I never wanted to hurt, and I was the one who hurt you more than any one person ever deserves. I'm so sorry." 
 If there's anything more crystal clear in this read, it has to be their undying love. It had never wavered. Not. For. One. Second! Now they've found each other again, he welcomes destiny with open arms. Grant realises forgiving her isn't an issue, literally grabs the bull by the horns and accepts what happened, happened. He knows the consequences will change his very existence but wait for it, something much bigger than he could ever have imagined sends this professional footballer built like a tank and invincible into a tailspin. Yep, she drops another bombshell! 
 "What are you trying to tell me?" "Just give it to me. I can take it. You don't need to ease me into this." 
 Grant is the best team member, the best player and the fastest. I loved Grant's inner-strength. Never once did he shy away from problems or responsibilities and tackled them like the brilliant sportsman he is. Confronted with the hardest game of their lives, these two lovers fight it together to win. Losing is not an option. Grant knows he's going to have to be stronger than ever because there's too much at stake. 
 "Despite whatever's come between us, you have always been and will always remain the closest thing to family I've ever had." 
 I had the immense pleasure of meeting one of the most unforgettable characters ever in this read. If I say any more about them, I would undoubtedly spoil this book for you which I have no wish in doing. Just one-click and you'll find out for yourselves who I'm talking about. My sista-in-arms, Rachel, asked me whether she should buy it or not. My answer was simple. God yes, it's a masterpiece! I was so invested in Ryan and Grant's story that stopping to highlight quotes or jot down notes was totally overlooked. After finishing, I went back in and virtually reread it. Ms Williams, you have written a gem of a book. I. Loved. It! The epilogue . . . WOW! I'll most definitely be reading Touching Down again. Another thing I'd like to mention is the author is donating ten percent of the net proceeds to charity. How cool is that! What can I say that I haven't already Nicole? BRAVO seems fitting! 
 "I like your book, Grant Turner." 
 "That's good. Since you're on every page in that book."

Short version: Sweet(ish) story with dark undertones, about first love between two geeky, outcast teens. It takes place in Omaha, Nebraska in 1986 and the chapters alternate between Eleanor's and Park's perspectives. While it is ultimately a story about two teens who find acceptance with each other, there are A LOT of serious issues crammed into this book: poverty, alcoholism, abuse, bullying, racism, masculinity and being Asian/biracial. It was darker than than the adorable book cover led me to believe. The handling of racial issues might bother some readers. It is a quick read. I am not overly enthusiastic about books centered on a couple falling in love, but the unconventional coupling and the touching portrayal of an awkward high school romance makes this one interesting. I am really curious about Rainbow Rowell's other work now. 
 Long version, spoilery: 
 But Park didn't have any luck--or status--to spare on that dumb redhead. He had just enough to keep himself out of trouble. And he knew it was crappy, but he was kind of grateful that people like that girl existed. Because people like Steve and Mikey and Tina existed, too, and they needed to be fed. If it wasn't that redhead, it was going to be somebody else. And if it wasn't somebody else, it was going to be Park. 
 Eleanor & Park takes place in Omaha, Nebraska during 1986. The first encounter between the two protagonists is on a school bus and they are really leery of one another. Over time they discover that they have shared interests and their relationship quickly picks up steam. The pull towards a person with similar interests is strong! (DID WE JUST BECOME BEST FRIENDS!?) Outside of their relationship, Eleanor is dealing with school bullying and an abusive stepfather and Park a Korean-American who feels like an outsider in a mostly white community and with his masculine father. 
 Disclaimer: I 'm not typically overly enthusiastic about books that center on a love story. I usually just like them rather than love them. I was hoping this book might be an exception. It wasn't, but there were a lot of aspects I really liked! The unconventional coupling is what made this book most interesting to me. Eleanor isn't stereotypically beautiful or undercover gorgeous. She is an average girl and Park is a geeky boy. They are both super awkward and they move at a slow pace physically. The alternating perspective was really effective, because we were able to see their inner thoughts contrasted with what actually came out of their mouths. Rainbow Rowell really captured that nervous, exciting feeling of first love! I loved viewing Eleanor and Park through each other's eyes, especially compared to how they saw themselves. 
 At first Park is scared how his classmates and family will view his relationship with Eleanor, but that attitude shifts as their relationship progresses. Park becomes the ideal sweet and super understanding boyfriend. (He reminded me a little of the perfect imaginary boyfriend from Inside Out: "I would DIE for Riley!" ) I could really relate to Eleanor's school life, where routine situations quickly turn into exercises of extreme humiliation! Eleanor's reaction when Park gives her a light makeover is so dramatic, but I can remember feeling the exact same way. ('I just, I look like I'm in costume. Like I'm trying to be something that I'm not.' Like she was trying to be pretty and popular. It was the trying part that was so disgusting.) She has a really self-deprecating and dry sense of humor that helps her deal with the constant barrage of bullying. ("The other girls all laughed, even the black girls who hated Tina. Laughing at Eleanor was Dr. King's mountain." Eleanor's way of saying that making fun of her brought people of all kinds together.) 
 Or maybe, he thought now, he just didn't recognize all those other girls. The way a computer drive will spit out a disk if it doesn't recognize the formatting. When he touched Eleanor's hand, he recognized her. He knew.(Park) 
 That feeling she used to have when she was sitting next to Park on the bus--that feeling that she was on base, that she was safe for the moment--she could summon it now. Like a force field. Like she was the Invisible Girl.(Eleanor) 
 The story of Eleanor's home and school life hit me harder than the romance, which was the center of the story. Eleanor has a really rough home life and I was really terrified for her. She had to keep strict schedule just so she could shower while her creepy, lurking stepdad was away. It was so sad how her mom was resigned to the situation. I think I started caring less about the love story because after the sweet build-up based on their common interests, the relationship became more about dramatic proclamations of love and awkward silences and arguments. The proclamations got really cloying towards the end! None of this is completely out of the ordinary for a first relationship, but the book loses some of its spark when the entire relationship become centered on conversations about the relationship and *~love~*. I would have liked more of the magic of the beginning sprinkled throughout. The constant mentions of Romeo and Juliet made me expect an end to be something a little bigger, so when I got to the end it felt anti-climatic and abrupt. 
 While ultimately this book is a first love story between two teens who find acceptance with each other, there are A LOT of serious issues crammed into this book: poverty, alcoholism, abuse, bullying, racism, masculinity and being biracial. It would have been nice to drop a few and explore some of them a little deeper. For instance Park's internalizing the media portrayals of Asians and "grass is always greener" attitude would have been interesting to explore, but I don't think he ever really came to terms with it. This book fell into some of the pitfalls of bringing up topics for background, but then providing enough details and supporting characters that the issues are brought them to the foreground, even though they were never meant to be a focus of the story. 
 (I am still working through my thoughts on this section, so it may make little to no sense!) I knew as soon as I finished reading that I would be able to find a lot of criticism of this book! Two of the most interesting articles I found are this post about problematic aspects and this defense of the book. There is a lot of casual racism in this book, mostly within context of the setting and the age group represented. The presence of racism did make the book feel more honest. These are high schoolers in a predominately white area, during a time not so long ago when it was much more difficult to get connected with the outside world. This 1986 version of Omaha isn't so different from my 1997 high school and I am assuming not completely different from now. Teenagers, and most adults to be completely honest, are still navigating the social landscape and pushing the limits of appropriateness. Zero filters! 
 It is really easy to side-eye some of Eleanor's thoughts about her "exotic" new boyfriend, though she did have enough awareness to keep her thoughts to herself most of the time! ("Park's eyes got wide. well, sort of wide. Sometimes she wondered if the shape of his eyes affected how he saw things. That was probably the most racist question of all time.") I do remember how many of my friends would focus on the single most identifying physical characteristic of their crushes and first boyfriends. I think Eleanor's mentions of Park's Asianness should have reduced as their relationship grew, rather than staying at the every-other-paragraph level. This book was just a snapshot in time and I imagine as she matures, so will her thought processes. As far as the selective bullying, some kids manage to escape the more aggressive bullying and others bear the full brunt. For that reason I didn't find it weird that Park seemed to escape mostly with microaggressions, especially with his connection to the popular crowd. Eleanor's very noticeable presence took the heat off some of the other targets, as she became the sole focus of the bullies. Fresh meat is always more fun to bullies, for a while anyway! 
 Some of the characters did manage to hit almost every stereotypical note. I didn't think it came from a place of a cruelty or that it was insight into the author's psyche, but it seemed unnecessary Some of these issues seemed like they would so easy to avoid, just by having a a more diverse set of character traits for at least a few of the characters. It struck me as especially odd that Park's mom seemed to have completely abandoned most aspects of her culture. As a single book none of this might matter so much, but in context with other works it starts to create the single narrative that gets repeated over and over until it crosses over from anecdote to the single, unimpeachable picture of an entire diverse culture. (See Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie: The Danger of a Single Story. It is short and definitely worth the read or listen!). I'm nitpicking on this book a little (I think Rowell is drawing from her experience and observations with her own community), but I think it is worth at least thinking about in this specific framework. 
 As far as the end, I sort of hated it at first! As I thought about it and let it settle in, I got it. Eleanor really did need space to heal and it is unlikely that Park would have understood. I like the little bit of hope in the end  and I am curious how these two character evolve. Rainbow Rowell did say she wasn't finished with these characters, so perhaps we will see! 
 This is definitely more than I ever expect I would have to say on this book and it obviously made me think about a wide range of issues! I will say that I am double the age of these characters and I probably would have loved this book in high school. If the first line of this review appeals to you or if you attended high school in the 80s, you'll appreciate this novel. It is a completely different story, but I'd like to mention Everything I Never Told You as a book that handles issues of race as part of a larger plot really well and I think it would appeal to YA readers. Anna Karenina remains my favorite portrayal of a couple falling in love (Levin's section, not Anna's :) ). 
 He tried again to remember what he'd thought the first time he saw her. He tried to remember how this had happened--how she went from someone he'd never met to the only one who mattered. (Park) 
 Ever since the first day they'd met, Eleanor was always seeing him in unexpected places. It was like their lives were overlapping lines, like they had their own gravity. Usually, that serendipity felt like the nicest thing the universe had ever done for her. (Eleanor)

 Tenley (Ten) is our heroine and I loved her zeal, her obsessions, and her steadfast beliefs. No one was going to coerce her into making a brash choice about her Everlife! From what I gathered, in this world, your Firstlife is the set up to help you live towards the rest of your Everlife. Everlife is split into two very different realms, Troika & Myraid, light & dark. Many people use their choices to bargain for a better Firstlife, for example, things like power, money, or the perfect job.  Confused? Yeah, like I said, super creative and really freaking interesting but damn is it hard to understand or explain. Also, why is her choice so important?! It gets deeper. 
 There is a war going on between the two Everlife realms and its effects can be felt on the current world. Each realm is fighting over many things, including recruits to build their armies to continue fighting each other. Her parents are running out of time to fulfill their contract, as it pertains to Ten, as she approaches 18, so they decide an asylum would be the perfect place to torture her into making her decision. The Death Cure. I'm sorry to say, my opinion of this book wasn't very high. The ending of this trilogy seemed nothing short of lazy. I'm going to start a mini rant now, so if you are interested in my opinion, read on, otherwise, feel free to skip to the next review. 
 In The Maze Runner, so much attention is focused on the nature of this project, on Thomas's fleeting memories, on the connection between Thomas and Teresa. And the stupid grievers. Well, apparently, all of that is irrelevant. We never find out what greater purpose Thomas served by going into the maze, Thomas never gets all of his memories back, the purpose of the grievers is never really revealed, and Teresa is basically non existent in this book. 
 In The Scorch Trials, so much of the focus was Thomas needing to feel betrayed by Teresa so they could get the right "patterns." But all of that was also completely pointless because the patterns are never truly elaborated on. Not to mention that for two books the chemistry between Teresa and Thomas was built, stretched and morphed, while Brenda was just thrust into the picture, and the only thing she had going for her was she was being touchy feely. 
 Finally, The Death Cure. The answer to all of our questions! How was The Maze Created, what made the creators decide a maze would help find the answers they needed, what caused the sun flares, what caused people to turn to cranks, what role did Thomas and Teresa play exactly, why was there a second maze for the girls, what memories were so important Wicked had no choice but to suppress them? By the time I finished the Scorch Trials, I was just so anxious to get my hands on this one because I just knew it was going to be epic. Wow, was I ever wrong. 
  Thomas adamantly refuses to get his memories back, so we never learn enough about who he was and why he was to truly form our opinion of why he did the things he did. Teresa was basically non existent in this book, and even though Brenda was always present, I never felt like I got to know her better, I never felt like she was a worthwhile part of the story. The cranks? Oh, there that way because a top secret government virus was accidently released during the sun flares. Want further elaboration on that? Good luck because there isn't any. Bite off Resident Evil much? Brenda tells Thomas he can only trust her and Chancellor Paige in this book, but we get no justification for either. Trust needs to be earned, not just stated loosely and then trusted blindly. The girls' maze, as well as the girls who were in it were not contingent to the story at all, and Aris, who was introduced as a major character in the second book only made an appearance in name. Teresa, a main protagonist in this trilogy? In addition to being practically non existent on the pages, she dies right near the end. A paragraph, if that is devoted to her death. What was the point of placing so much emphasis on her role just to kill her off, just like that? Again, completely pointless. All so Thomas, Brenda, and about 200 other immunes could escape to the last known paradise in the world. NO results came of any of the trials. Then a new villainous force was introduced in the form of the right arm, which was also a meaningless addition to the story. This book was not at all well thought out or crafted. The only part of this entire book that was halfway decent was Thomas having to kill Newt so he wouldn't turn into a full blown crank. That was the only part that at least felt sincere.  
 Basically, this entire trilogy could have been condensed into a maximum of two books, and honestly, I disliked the conclusion so much that I am going back and reducing the ratings on the first two books, simply because they built up to nothing. I don't recommend this book if you want a book with a thoughtfully laid out conclusion, but hey, every opinion is different and this is just mine.

 A pretty significant part of Jalan's past (and that of the Red Queen's) was fleshed out in this sequel; including the event that probably precipitated his tendencies for blanking out unpleasantness. These 'flashbacks' provided context to the extent of the Red Queen's War, Jalan's true lineage, and also finally introducing us to the enigmatic Lady Blue. 
 The two new prominent characters travelling with Jalan and Snorri, i.e. Kara and Hennan, were also memorable in their own right. Although at times I felt that they seemed to serve as fodder to Jalan's character development more than anything else within the plot, particularly Hennan. 
 In spite of the humour, however, this is by no means light-hearted fantasy. There were a few truly heart-wrenching scenes, disturbing displays of necromancy and a pervasive sense of darkness surrounding the Broken Empire. And of course, plenty of references to Jorg Ancrath here too. 
 The Liar's Key is a much longer book than Prince of Fools, and the pacing was still uneven with a lot of travelling involved even though it has a good dose of action throughout. We do finally get to witness the strange power of Loki's Key in various situations. However, the worldbuilding started to feel weird especially when Jalan ventured into Florence and the whole financial system really jars with the medieval-like setting. It is still a worthy sequel in my opinion, and regrettably now I have to wait till June next year for the finale.

Suddenly she is a Sassenach--an "outlander"--in a Scotland torn by war and raiding border clans in the year of Our Lord...1743. 
 Hurled back in time by forces she cannot understand, Claire is catapulted into the intrigues of lairds and spies that may threaten her life...and shatter her heart. For here James Fraser, a gallant young Scots warrior, shows her a love so absolute that Claire becomes a woman torn between fidelity and desire...and between two vastly different men in two irreconcilable lives. 
 Ok, so this was a book that I've kind of wanted to read for a while. Then when several of my friends started raving about the show, I figured it was time that I give this a shot. And boy am I glad I did! This book had action, adventure, romance, heartache, revulsion and just the slightest dash of horror.

I loved Jamie's vows to protect Claire and the fact that he proved it time and again. I also loved watching Jamie's leadership skills. He was such a great leader in general, from the first time he's introduced to Claire and all their interactions at Leoch, through the wedding and their stay at Lallybroch. He proved that he'll protect not only Claire, but those that fall under his protection with everything he has (although I think he went about five steps further when it came to Claire, but that's besides the point). I loved Claire's character. She was sassy, smart, witty (and while she did annoy the tiniest bit a couple of times), she also didn't let the story get boring. And of course when coupled with Jamie who was himself sassy, stubborn and so very swoony, they were just great! 
 Black Jack Randall was the worst sort of villain. He contributed to the revulsion and horror that I mentioned earlier. I did feel bad for Claire, considering that Black Jack looked so much like Frank. But considering everything he did, I'm glad she was able to finally get to a point where she could look at Black Jack and not see Frank. 
 I want to know more about how Claire handles her interesting dilemma. With her knowledge, if she's says something to even just Jamie, she could potentially change things. Of course (like Anselm says), just by being in 1743 there's some changes she may have already made.

I definitely liked this one better than Mine Till Midnight. I honestly really enjoyed reading it, but there were a few things that bugged me enough to where I just can't give this five stars. 
 What I liked: 
 Kleypas can write some serious sizzle. The connection between Kev and Win leaps off the page. Every glance and expression and touch has meaning and emotion, and it's intense. I thought all of their love scenes were incredibly well done. I also liked reading about their past, diving into Win's illness into more detail. Their bond felt much stronger to me than Cam/Amelia's for having a longer, more entwined history. I really like HR's where the characters have always known they were supposed to be together someday. This was truly the strength of this book, and the first and foremost reason I enjoyed reading it overall. I like some brooding, angsty romance from time to time when it's done right. 
 I liked Win a lot. She had a lot of inner strength and determination that drove her to conquer her illness and not compromise on what she wanted. I was glad when she stood up to Kev about halfway through, showing that she wouldn't even let him tell her what she could or couldn't do. 
 At times, I really enjoyed the Hathaway family dynamics. There were funny moments with the sisters...and dare I say it, Leo. He came a longggg way in this book from where he was in the first one. (Where I wanted to stab him in the face repeatedly for being the most miserable coward and endangering his entire family.) I do feel like Kleypas has a tendency to over-include characters from previous titles in her books...as if they're doing a TV reunion special or something. I know some people really like that, but I think it makes the books feel a bit cheesy in a way. I'm fine with some connections throughout, but I want the story to focus on the characters at hand. 
 What I didn't like so much: 
 Kev came off as a total ass for a decent portion of the book. There were times when he was fabulous- caring for Win when she was so sick, putting aside differences to jump to the rescue, the whole finally carrying Win off to the woods thing (although there was an air of sexism there that can't be ignored), and how he was upon their eventual and expected HEA- all of that was great. But, there were times when I just couldn't understand what Win even wanted with him. He spent a good portion of the middle of the book just sulking and brooding and growling and barely speaking. He wouldn't let himself have Win, but he wouldn't let anyone else, either. That's unfair and...dickish, really. He would forget himself and start to ravish her and then shove her away. I mean, what an ass. I couldn't understand why he insisted that he couldn't be with her, especially since he was supposed to love her, and that's all she ever really wanted. I got frustrated for a while, and honestly lost some hope of him redeeming himself. I suppose he mostly did, but he never apologized for acting like that, and I feel like he should have. I know Win lied to him, which isn't good either, but his behavior cheesed me off for quite a while. 
 I didn't mind the whole figuring out Cam's and Kev's origins side plot, but I felt like things wrapped up a little too easily and neatly with a big ol' bow, especially with  Kev ending up being the heir to a title and a crapton of Irish lands and properties. I would've been happy just to see him and Win live in the way that he'd described- in a home he would build for them.  I mean, what were the odds that everyone would figure out the connection and be present for them to work it all out? 
 In the end, I read through this pretty darn quickly, didn't want to put it down, and did really enjoy it. I'm glad I read it before trying Tempt me at Twilight, since all of the characters do seem to be making appearances that may not be necessary to catch, but I think will enhance the reading of the subsequent titles. (There was a lot of groundwork here for Leo's title, btw. Like, a lot.) I would definitely recommend reading them all and in order, which is what I plan to keep doing.

I rarely find myself venturing into the world of magic realism because past experience has resulted in me finding it rather disengaging, a little silly, and frankly just not my taste. However, I was drawn in by the premise of this novel and hoped that it would mark a change for my relationship with the style. On this it has; I truly enjoyed this novel. The Strange and Beautiful Sorrows of Ava Lavender lives up to its name in many ways, being both strange and very beautiful. It is undeniably unique and was a reading experience like no other. 
 Ava Lavender tells this story like a multi-generational memoir in her own voice, making her the narrator and the ultimate centre of the story but drawing her mother, Viviane, and maternal grandmother, Emilienne, in as vivid and vital characters in their own right. Ava tells of each woman's life, focusing especially on each's loves and sorrows and the need for freedom from various traps and cages. Over the course of the narrative, all three women become more intriguing and more understandable, more familiar and yet also more mysterious. It is an excellent balance that suits the story so well. Each of the characters explored in the novel - not just these three central women - is undeniably strange in some way or another and has some kind of important effect on the lives of Emilienne, Viviane, and/or Ava. Watching this play out the way it does was truly engaging as they all struggle with what life throws their way. 
 Once again being true to its name, this novel has a strand of sorrow that weaves its way throughout the entire narrative. It displays itself more prominently in many ways (often related to love) but is clearly present during the whole story and adds a great deal to the feeling of the novel. The emotions that rise and fall in the telling of this story were one of the most powerful parts for me. I felt they were woven so well together and the memoir format helps bring them alive in the forefront. The love that comes and goes and the family bond that quietly permeates so many of the interactions feel so honest that I couldn't help but feel affected. 
 The magic realism was, to me, handled with a light hand and a subtle touch and I think that is why I enjoyed it significantly more than I often do. There were occasions where something especially peculiar pulled me out of the story a bit, but someone used to the quirks of magic realism I think would find this an enjoyable adventure throughout. 
 This novel really is so unique and immersive. The narrative is one that slowly pulls you deep into these characters' lives so you become invested almost without realizing, and yet also manages to maintain a distance that strikes a masterful balance. If you're looking for a sorrowful, beautifully written tale of human hearts and all the good and bad they take, this is the novel for you. If you're looking for YA with a very literary feel, this one is for you. Even if you're looking for a book set in the past that is not at all about the history, this book is for you. All these wonderful elements blend together so well to create this wonderful piece of literature. For a style that I do not often enjoy, this one truly took me by surprise.

Brutal. 
 This book in one word is Brutal with a capital B. I had started reading this book a few months back but within the first few pages I realized I wasn't in the mood for this kind of book. I am so very glad I came back to it when my mood changed. If you like war games set against a sci-fi/fantasy backdrop, with well-developed characters, and a compelling story of overcoming a corrupt political system then this book is written for you. 
 Red Rising is a story about a young man that lives a simple life of work and family and love. Darrow is talented; among the best at what he does despite his young age, so he has some standing among his tribe, but he is destined for a hard short life in a harsh unforgiving world full of rules and little rewards. But he has Eo, his equally young but wise beyond her years wife and the love he has for her gives him purpose. 
 And then she is taken from him in one of the cruelest ways I have ever read. This scene wrecked me. I can't even imagine having to be a participant in the death of a loved one.  So, understandably, he goes a little off the rails. He doesn't just want revenge against the man that took her away from him; he wants to bring down the whole damn system in blazing ball of fire and ash. And of course there are people ready and waiting to ignite that fire. 
 After Darrow finds out everything he has ever believed was a lie he allows himself to become a weapon for the cause. He has been hollowed out by the death of Eo, so it is easy for the Sons of Ares to fill him with the skills he will need to infiltrate the ranks of the elite that have enslaved them. He becomes a goddamn gladiator and marches willingly into the coliseum with the lions because to not live this lie to the fullest will mean failure to fulfill Eo's dream and avenge her death. 
 Just. So. Amazing. 
 There are so many things I enjoyed about this book... 
 First, the characters all have enormous depth. With the exception of maybe Darrow, but he lost his ability to depth the day he pulled his wife's legs to make her suffering less and now has a single-minded goal of destruction guiding his every decision. Although there was character development on his part, I needed him to remain the wrath of the movement to stay true to the character he became the day Eo died.  The women of this novel are strong. Like, really strong in terms of perseverance, intelligence, resourcefulness, and bravery (not to mention they are deadly as all hell). I would have liked to have seen what a house of only women warriors would have looked like to Pierce in this story. But that's almost the beauty of this world because among the elites, the women are just as formidable as the men and to underestimate them would mean your death. I get the sense they wouldn't have ever even considered a house of only male warriors superior to a house of only female warriors so we get equal opportunity murder and mayhem for this version of life on Mars. Darrow's lieutenants are fascinating; I love them all for different reasons. This book could have easily devolved into a mindless bloodbath, but there is so much STRATEGY and build throughout the book that I was completely pulled into the lives of these people. 
 There is Action! This book is not for the squeamish; there is blood, and lots of it. I have heard people compare this to The Hunger Games, and I sort of get it because there are 12 districts/12 houses and fights to the death among a group of teens in a "game" setting, but really that is where the comparison ends. I LOVED The Hunger Games, but I am also falling hard for Red Rising. 
 The world of Red Rising is interesting and unique. Caste systems are not a new concept, making other planets hospitable for human life is not a new concept, fighting against the system is NOT a new concept. Yet, Pierce Brown has managed to take all of these "not new" concepts and make them shiny and new and exciting all over again. There is some jargon used in the book that is a little hard to get through it at first (this is the reason I walked away from the books a few months ago and knew it was not what I needed right then) and there is significant world building that has to happen for the story make sense. It doesn't all get explained early on, but it is revealed to you as it is revealed to Darrow so there is a method to it and some of the dreaded info-dumping is there, but not as bad as it could be for a book like this. I think it was all written very well. 
 There is very little romance. Darrow's one true love's death is what sets this whole book in motion very early on in the story so despite there being temptation along the way, he doesn't acknowledge it, much. There is some "off screen" romance between a few secondary characters, but if you are looking for a break from insta-love, then this is going to be a perfect fit. 
 There were also some pieces that didn't quite fit for me... 
 They put so much effort into making Darrow perfect. Like painful surgery after surgery, body mods on top of layers of more body mods. His bones, his muscles, his eyes, his hair, his skin, you name it and it is scraped off and replaced (and it is described in painful detail). But, if perfection is the goal for the entire society of elite leaders (the Golds), why do not more of them do this? They feed him enhancers to increase the rate at which he can build muscle, and even increase his ability to retain force-fed intelligence. But why don't they all do it? 
 There were two other bits that annoyed me but they didn't ruin my enjoyment of the story and they are pretty big spoilers. DON"T CLICK THE SPOILER LINK if you don't want to know. I'm serious damn it, it could ruin the reading experience for you.  1) How could Dancer not know that Titus had made it into the school, and if he knew, why the hell didn't he tell Darrow? They could have been strong allies from the start and would have bettered their chances of success in the games. 2) How did none of the potential benefactors notice what was happening in the games with the proctors showing favor to the Jackal? It was clear that Darrow had won Priam for his house, but then was never served the honor because the proctors wouldn't allow it. I feel like they would have seen these games play out frequently enough before that they would recognize what was happening.   
 Overall, this book was everything I needed it to be when I needed it to be it. It may not be that for everyone who reads it, but do yourself a favor and wait until your mood is right before you pick it up because once you do, you won't be able to put it down. For me this is a 4.5 rounded up to a 5 because I was actually surprised at how much I liked it and only got one hour of sleep last night because I couldn't stop reading.

Okay, I'll admit it: The blurb on this novel didn't win me over. 
 But since author Jessica Park raved about Aspen on her Facebook page, I decided to give it a chance--especially when I saw that it was available through NetGalley. And the rest, as they say, is history. 
 This powerful narrative of self-discovery, friendship, and love completely blew me away. Aspen, our heroine, is a phenomenal character. But the secondary characters are equally compelling. While I can certainly accept this as a standalone, I'd love to see a sequel featuring Kim and Cass (with glimpses of Ben, Ninny, and Aspen, of course). 
 The first thing I noticed about Crane's novel was its realistic portrayal of teenagers and the high school experience. The author establishes a disparity between Aspen's perception of herself and how others see her, which--while always the case to some degree--is perhaps most evident during these formative years. 
 Aspen is notably insecure regarding her appearance, especially her hair--"the curly, dirty blonde mess that protrudes from my head, like a perm on a troll doll"--which prevents her from blending in with her peers. Nevertheless, she is relatively content with her status on campus: While she has a small group of loyal friends, she's not what anyone would term popular--that is, until an unfortunate accident catapults her into unwelcome stardom. 
 Navigating this new phenomenon only adds to her list of problems, which already consists of dealing with stress-induced migraines, processing her reaction to the trauma, and hallucinating a dead person. So her emphasis on using the right word(s) is indicative of a need to restore order to a chaotic, unpredictable life. After all, definitions are black and white (quite literally, in fact, if one considers how they're printed on a dictionary page). 
 Readers are kept in suspense regarding the real story behind the accident, and it's only through the combined effort of Aspen, her newfound friends, and her therapist, that our title character is able to piece together the night's events. 
 One of my favorite aspects of the novel is the witty dialogue that takes place between Aspen and her friends, and between Aspen and Ben. I laughed out loud at how unexpected and comical some of these conversations were. (If only I could be so clever! Alas, I'm unsure how to cultivate or hone this skill.) But beyond being funny, these exchanges demonstrate how smart, well-informed, and good-natured this cast of characters is at its core. 
 For me, Aspen is the perfect balance of light and heavy. Both Ninny's eccentricity and the playful banter between characters seem to counter the novel's darker moments, while the supportive Suzy and Kim counteract the venomous Olivia and Claire. In addition, Aspen treats concepts such as identity, friendship, romance, and family with the honesty and reverence they deserve. 
 Overall, Aspen is a gripping, emotional read that is so real, so profound in its simplicity, that it will have you reading compulsively until the very last page.

I gave this book two stars because of the strengths it shares with the first two books in the series: it's intriguing, has fascinating characters, and has a unique plot and setting (rural western Virginia rather than a big city or beach town). But unlike the first two books in The Raven Cycle, Blue Lily, Lily Blue has flaws that are difficult to overlook this time, the most important being that this is clearly a book of fillers. 
 After a book as well-executed (in this reviewer's opinion) as The Dream Thieves, it was almost jarring to see how erratic the pacing was this time around. Rather than answering questions presented in the last book, BLLB instead introduces new questions that are clearly left open so that they can come up again in the last book. Of all the stories effected by this, Adam's suffers the most. We are reminded on virtually every page that he was abused, but we never actually learn anything about his life before Aglionby or anything that really defines him beyond his abuse--for a character that fixes cars like a pro, is intelligent and well-read, and is acutely aware of all that is going on around him, this is especially disappointing. His trial scene is perhaps the most frustrating: after vaguely worrying about facing his father in court, Adam is spontaneously joined by his friends--how they found out about the case and managed to somehow show up precisely as the trial began is not revealed--only to have the scene cut off and the verdict not revealed, neither by thought or conversation, in the hundred pages that follow.* This is only made worse by Adam's constantly shifting thoughts and emotions throughout the second half of the novel. For a fairly outwardly collected character, this creates an awkward advancement, and his "awakening" at the novel's conclusion feels rushed and out of place. 
 Although I'd argue that each of the main characters is still lovable in their own way, it's more difficult to sympathize with the group at this point. Despite being arguably the most heavily focused on character, Blue is also quickly becoming one of the series' weakest points. Despite telling us herself in the first book that she's clearly a judgmental person, Blue is never called out for her actions. She is extremely critical of both Gansey and Adam, often unreasonably, but is never urged to apologize or admit that she is wrong. Her romantic relationship with Gansey--which we are told from day one is destined to be true love--is still rather unconvincing. Surprisingly, Adam and Ronan's relationship, which isn't even yet canon, is more believable than our other pair's: we've seen them talk, argue, interact around other people as well as the paranormal, do mundane tasks such as going to class or to the grocery store, and confide in each other. By contrast, Gansey and Blue only spend time alone together when it's in the romantic context, and neither seem to really know anything about each other that the other characters don't know already. Their love story is an forced one, and it's hard to see how two characters so fundamentally different from one another (especially when one party--Blue--critiques the other to the point that arguably borders on mistreatment) could have a long-lasting relationship. 
 Lastly, BLLB does nothing to establish why we should care about the characters' mystical quest in the first place. Cabeswater still doesn't have much of a purpose, and why on Earth anyone would want to wake up Glendower is a mystery, since we're given no reason for why he needs to be woken or what he's going to do once he's awake. Then there is The Grey Man, a hit man who is apparently in the midst of a redemption arc despite never showing any remorse, and who is shown universal respect by the other characters despite having been the one who killed Ronan's father. 
 The truth of the matter is, if you enjoyed the first two books and adore the characters, as I do, you'll still enjoy reading BLLB. But once the original read is finished, there's no denying that it could have been better. 
 *Update: to further elaborate on why the trial scene particularly bothered me so much, there were several reasons: 
 1) It was probably the biggest deux ex machina in the series thus far. Gansey and Ronan show up precisely as Adam's trial begins, and there's really no clue as to how they found out that the trial was that day. It's clear that the author set this up for emotional impact, but the level of happenstance prevents it from being very effective. 
 2) As many other people have mentioned, Adam has some sort of epiphany in this scene where he decides that Gansey was right all along and that he only wants to help Adam out because they're friends, not as a means to control him. This certainly sounds great, but it also (probably unintentionally) puts all the blame on Adam. Gansey may be a nice guy, but he has he flaws too, and to portray all their disagreements as Adam's fault is frustrating and unfulfilling. 
 3) Out of everything that happened in this book, what bothered me the most was how Ms. Stiefvater decided to have Gansey be a friend of the judge presiding over the case. We see Gansey come swaggering in, shaking the judge's hand, making small talk about their home lives, and doing his politician charade. We know that Adam was assaulted, so again we're supposed to think this is a great thing, for Gansey to defend his abused friend. However, what we rather get is an example of a wealthy teenager using power and wealth to influence a legal case. The verdict sits on the fact that Gansey Has Connections, and not on Adam, who is doing something incredibly brave and heart-breaking. It also seems like the author is glorifying this use of power, and simply because we already know and care about Gansey doesn't make this any less disturbing.

ORIGINAL POST: RULES OF CIVILITY by Amor Towles: Best Friends for Now 
 http://fangswandsandfairydust.com/201... on August 12, 2015 
 ARC obtained anonymously at BEA. No remuneration was exchanged and all opinions presented herein are my own except as noted. 
 I picked this book up anonymously at BEA. Frankly it sat on my shelf and I didn;t think I would get to it during my blogging career. But, someone chose it for my book club so here I am. It is "literary fiction," so is probably intended to be critiqued in all sorts of esoteric manners. 
 This book is about a lot of things. Like a contemporary romance featuring youngish people, the times were tough, people were on the end of the Great Depression and an economic relapse and on the verge of WWII (with forays into the Spanish Civil War). Social roles were changing and our classless society was both stratifying and dissolving. Like the books wherein people in their 20s and 30s try to find direction in contemporary times, this book deals with similar choices and issues. It also nods to great writers of the story's time period (pre-WWII): Fitzgerald, Rand, Parker, etc. 
 Have you ever had friends you thought you would have forever, the friends you thought really knew you to the bottom of your soul and you them? I'm not talking about the girls you met at sleep-away camp when you were teens, but the friend you met as an adult, who you treated as a sister, and who then blew you off, or who inexplicably changed personalities? This story, for me spoke directly to the fickle nature of some friendship; especially as we become adults. 
 I felt as if this book rambled a lot: at times I thought it wasn't really going anywhere. But one thing leads to another, one "minor" encounter can have remarkably long lasting effects. It was unusual in its punctuation; avoiding those pesky quotation marks. 
 Katey is something interesting: well read, smart, amply skilled in shorthand and such, clever, with ambiguous morals. If she had been a man at the time, the world would have been her oyster. But, as one woman tells her in the book she shouldn't worry about what the guy she ends up with is going to do, but what she is going to do. 
 It was one of those times when the pendulum was swinging forward for women, and society women were more hampered by norms than the women who had built themselves up from nothing were. Katey had no expectations from friends or family -- she appears to have had neither between her father's death and the time of the story. In a sense she is a blank slate upon which the twentieth century gets to write its story of what a working woman is. She is also without a social past, and through coincidence becomes like a visitor to another planet as she enters social circles higher than those of her birth and status. 
 While unquestionably Katey is the heroine of this story, she is morally ambiguous. She isn't a bad person, but she's no Mother Theresa. 
 This is the second book in one week I read about the same period of time, with the other occurring in England. I felt in each though that the women were dispassionate, husks really, waiting for a man, or at least love, to make their lives begin. Of course each learns that is not how one's life is made complete but it is the premium toppings on the sundae. 
 Katey has the sense to go on living and progressing without the necessity of a man, although she still has the tendency towards wanting one. But, getting in on the ground floor of a new magazine, she is the "new woman;" like Katherine Hepburn in a slew of movies (although her popularity was a little later), she could become the first Helen Gurley Brown if she stayed focused. 
 The "Rules of Civility' refer to a text attributed to George Washington setting forth rules every young man should aspire to follow. 
 But this book is about a lot of things -- some are obvious and others are not. I found it slow to start but easy to read. And, I find I keep thinking about it and what it means. It is strange and modern, and yet ordinary and classic. Highly recommend.

Fifteen-year-old Meredith ("Chirp") is coming undone because her father, who sexually molested and raped her when she was twelve, is coming home from prison. 
 It's clear from the outset of Such a Pretty Girl that Meredith's mother will not protect her. She's just way too excited about her husband's homecoming and can't understand why Meredith isn't showing enthusiasm. This even though she knows that her husband raped her daughter. Three years earlier, at the hospital, she told the bleeding Meredith not to tell anyone, that dad, like all people, makes mistakes 
 The whole neighborhood knows that a sexual predator is coming home and almost everyone resents his presence, fears what he will do to their children, and--in the 'blame the victim' model--stays clear of Meredith. However, she does have some supporters--Nigel, the cop who arrested Charles on the night of the rape, and Andy and his mom Mrs. Mues. Andy has also been raped by Charles. After a later accident, Andy is inexplicably paralyzed from the waist down. He and Meredith are boyfriend and girlfriend. 
 The entire story takes place over the course of a few days with Meredith having lots of italicized flashbacks to scenes of her father both being a good dad (when she was very young) and a sexual predator. No matter how she tries to sort out what is happening to her, she feels that she will have to be victimized again in order to put her dad back in jail, and that no one will be able to help her. 
 Is she right? 
 High school housekeeping: Such a Pretty Girl is a tight little novel--both short and physically compact, it's very portable. It's an easy read, somewhere in the sixth grade level, although its content is clearly meant for older teens. I recommend it for most high school students, but I think it will have particular appeal to reluctant readers. 
 I'm not sure how students will reaction to Meredith's mom. By anyone's measure, she is one dimensional--entirely shallow, worried about keeping up with the Joneses (without recognizing how all the Joneses hate her), concerned about her fading good looks, and completely out of touch with the damage child sexual abuse does to her daughter. She serves as a mouthpiece for details of setting, so her unnatural conversation may be disconcerting. The reader doesn't know why she is so oblivious when her own mother (Meredith's grandmother) is much more centered. I attributed it to the fact that her husband brainwashed her so early. (They began dating when she was twelve.) However, she's a good villain--showing her own evil is banal and entirely unlike her husband's. She does tremendous damage just by not stepping up as a mom. She the kind of person we love to hate.

This novel took a really long time to become interesting to me. We start off right at the beginning, at Lada's birth and then her younger brother Radu's and we follow them through their early childhood and younger years when they then get left by their father as collateral damage at the enemies hands. When you're reading this first half you can't see why on earth we need this much detail into their lives, it's dry, it's long and I felt like I was slugging through but I stuck with it after being told things pick up at around page 200. And that person was right, it does. But also in the second half I learned to appreciate the first half, that half that I'd dragged myself through, as it fleshed out the characters. You could understand their motivations, their reasons and their flaws and I don't think that would have been as strong if we weren't with these two from the very beginning. 
 Lada is mean, strong and determined. Women are inferiors and she refuses to let her father treat her that way, so she becomes fierce and quite feral actually in an effort to be seen. Throughout the whole novel Lada is anti-women, she hates going to the baths with the women, the gossiping and girl-talk but she especially hates that women are a mans property and she will do everything in her power to never let that happen to herself. She gets offended when the men in her party make any reference to her being female and I found it to be a little anti-women at some points. I get that Lada wants to be a strong, independent person but why can't she also be a woman and pave the way for other women to follow? 
 Radu is the sweet, charming, caring and emotional little brother. He gets stepped on by everyone and taunted by his sister and her friend. He is the little piece of sunshine in this story but he never really gets his moment. I really want to see Radu happy in the next installment. 
 Definitely though the turning point for this book is around when Mehmed, the Sultan's son, enters the story. Having an ally brings new adventures for both Lada and Radu. From that point this story really picks up and Lada and Radu find their place in their new home. 
 As much as I did complain earlier that this book is a little too detailed there were some parts that were really interesting to read such as the politics and religions of the empire. I haven't read many (if any....?) books with Islam featured and it surprised me when I got angry at Lada for being so closed minded. I'm all for equality, freedom and acceptance in the debates currently going on in the world and especially the divide in my own home town about construction of new places of worship, so to see that featured in a YA novel really resonated with me. 
 Because this world is so complex, I'm a bit annoyed I read this before the rest of the series is published. This is definitely one I'm going to have to reread to immerse myself back in this story before picking up book 2. I'm glad though that I did give this book a chance, the first 200 pages at the time felt like a 1 or 2 star read but when the story picked up it had me hooked and I have to give it 4 stars now.

 So, I've just marathoned the Adrien English series adn I am in love. 
 In love with Adrien. 
 In love with Jake 
 and in love with Josh Lanyon's writing. 
 I know I'm a decade behind everyone else. I know, okay. The important thing is I've realised the error of my ways and am rectifying the situation by consuming Lanyon's words as quickly as possible. As I didn't review each book of this series separately, I'm going to do one review for books 2-5. I did read 1 ages ago, but was obviously a real doofus who didn't catch on to the beauty of this writing! 
 The thing about this series is the central character Adrien and his, seemingly, doomed love for Jake - the totally in the closet cop. While each book has a fantastic mystery to read and try and solve, it is Adrien and Jake's relationship that kept me hooked and needing to know more. 
 I adored Adrien and his witty observations and curious attitude. I loved Jake and his tough cop persona but together... 
 Oh how I loved their relationship. 
 Even when I hated it. 
 Why? Why did I love it so much? It contained all the things I shouldn't like. A closeted cop. Cheating. Blatant cheating and an off the page woman getting conned into a relationship, a marriage, because Jake hated himself for being gay. 
 I should abhor it. I do, really, in black and white, I would say there is no forgiveness for Jake and Adrien's actions - particularly once Kate was pregnant and Jake had got married. So why was I still devouring it? Wanting more? Desperately wishing Adrien and Jake would have an HEA?? 
 Basically because of Lanyon's writing. He made me see the real people beneath the black and white, right and wrong. 
 Yes, it is wrong to cheat. As civilised human beings we need to consider the feelings of others and not just our own wants and needs. That's not to say we shouldn't pursue what we want but...oh hell, y'all know what I'm saying, right? Cheating is not a nice thing to do. 
 I didn't like Jake for cheating. I didn't like Adrien for being the one Jake cheated with when he knew the situation. 
 And yet I understood it. 
 For all that it was wrong, the fact is, all of the characters in this book were in pain. Jake from the self hatred he carries round - if he can't accept himself as being gay, how will anyone else? To be so despising of your own self...well, I found that the saddest thing of all. I hated that Kate was 'collateral damage' in his fight to come to terms with who he was and who he loved. Well, not who he was, because gay or straight or bi, he was still Jake. He was still the cop. He was still the man the world saw, he just couldn't admit that the man the world saw had fallen in love with another man. 
 It's funny how it was the falling in love that tripped him up. He was happy enough to spend his time in S&M clubs, gay S&M clubs. U=It wasn't the sex, but the feelings, the emotion that he couldn't deal with. 
 Yes his job was partly why he stayed closeted. 
 Yes his family was another part of why he stayed closeted. 
 But really it was only himself who he was hiding from. When he needed the strength to admit what he felt for Adrien. When it literally became life and death, he stepped up tot he mark. 
 Sorry, I didn't mean this to turn into a complete analysis of Jake and his actions!! It obviously struck a chord with me, that even the strongest of people have fears and event he strongest of people hurt those they least want to hurt. We are humans and humans are not perfect and are far from infallible. 
 Lanyon portrays this so well. And he manages to do it while adding humour and mystery to his stories. As I'm probably the last person on the planet to actually read these books, I doubt I have anyone left to recommend them too - but I do, if like me, you've been under a rock. Read these. They're good. 
 (Also, the audio versions are excellent).

 I am not a novella kind-a girl. To me, they are just a money grubbing scheme to get more money by flogging a dead horse. They do not appeal to me, even in series I like. However, I did purchase Assassin's Blade as a bundle deal purchase and well....damn 
 Assassin's Blade is composed of 5 novella's that blend so beautifully together that is does read like a novel. That in itself made me impressed. You want to know what else impressed me. It focused on Celaena and how she came to be when we first meet her in Throne of Glass, all the while not spoiling Throne of Glass or any of the other books. Now, let me say this now, I read this before reading Throne of Glass, so I had little to no knowledge of what the hell was happening apart from awesome assassin kicking some ass. 
 I am going to review each novella on its own merit. 
 The Assassin and the Pirate Lord: 5 bookmarks 
 It took me awhile to get into the swing of things, but like beginning with any new novel where the characters are all new to you, that was expected. When I finally fell into my groove, I was grinning from ear to ear as I took in every word. 
 I went in expecting some cold heartless assassin and Celaena is like that but with this novella you see there is a person within that killing machine exterior. I liked that- I LOVED that. It made Celaena complex, made her more real and by far a more interesting character. Sure, seeing her killing and doing what she has been trained to do is awesome, but if she didn't have some form of compassion she would fail as a character. 
 The Assassin and the Healer: 4.5 bookmarks 
 This story is the result of her actions in The Assassin and the Pirate Lord. In traveling to the Silent Assassin's, she encounters a young barmaid and helps her in her time of need. The only reason I gave this 4.5 bookmarks isn't because it was written any less beautifully, or that Celaena's character had dramatically change. To me, the story didn't fit in. I know it is there so when a time comes in the series and we see the barmaid again, which I am assuming will happen, we will know her and Celaena's backstory. But it was a bit long for something that really didn't move the story forward. 
 The Assassin and the Desert: 5 bookmarks 
 ASSASSIN'S!!!! So many assassin's in one place and nothing happens! Haha So if nothing happens, why in the hell did I give it 5 bookmarks? Because there is SO much character development. Celaena makes her first, true friend...ever. To me that was a MAJOR growth for her character. She opened up to her and was quickly reminded why she never does. This story resounded with me, I think about it constantly. So much happens that shapes Celaena and I love it. 
 The Assassin and the Underworld: 5 bookmarks 
 We are finally given what we came for. Celaena assassinating people! We she her at a vulnerable stage where she realizes that she isn't invincible. I liked this story, I really did. Again, you get a new look at Celaena, dig deeper into the complexity of her character. 
 The Assassin and the Empire: 5 bookmarks and a vile of my tears as an offering 
 I'm not even...I can't. 
 My heart has been torn out, smashed into pieces before my eyes punted across the room. The only other time I have ever-EVER cried whist reading was Deathly Hallows when Fred died, and then again when Snape died. Congratulations Sarah J. Maas, you have made the teeny tiny list of authors who have made me tear up and sob like a child. Well done you, not sure if I hate you or admire you. Characters that I knew so little about, was still becoming invested in held that impact on me. 
 Sarah J. Mass all I want to say is, you have quickly become a favourite author of mine...

 "Was it really some other person I was so anxious to discover, when I did all of that looking, or was it only my own solitude that I could not abide?" 
 Wittgenstein's Mistress is about a woman who may or may not be the last woman on earth - who may or may not have traveled across Eastern and Western Europe, the United States and Mexico. She may or may not have had a husband named Adam and a son named Simon. She may or may not have seen a cat in the Colliseum in Rome. She may or may not have survived by building fires and living in large, famous museums all over the world. Alone. 
 I liked this mostly for the idea of it. It's stream of consciousness wandering and references to art, history and literature can be challenging. Given the nature and style of the book, it's no wonder that it encountered 54 rejections before finally getting published. Mel recommended it to me because I liked the style of Wittgenstein's Tractatus - and the style, though not overtly similar, has a consonant feel. A narrative of trying to organize and defend one's thoughts against chaos. 
 In the Afterword, Wittgenstein's Mistress is described as the best illustration of Wittgenstein's proposition that "philosophy is a battle against the bewitchment of our intelligence by means of language." Throughout Kate's stream of consciousness rambling, she makes connections weaving together paintings, classic epic poems, buildings and the like - any or all of which might be incorrect and mis-remembered, and she struggles with this through the entire narrative. She frequently loses track of things she wanted to remember, and then picks up the thread later to almost comic relief. 
 For those who value such facts, Wittgenstein is most frequently mentioned (after the two quotes at the beginning) in Kate's narrative in reference to his interactions with Bertrand Russell, to whether or not Wittgenstein played an instrument and which one, and to the fact that (Kate believes she read) the Wittgenstein never read a word of Aristotle. 
 UPDATE: Okay, I just had to add one more quote that I love, and then really I'm through with this review. Really. 
 Surely if Wittgenstein was as intelligent as one was generally led to believe he ought to have been able to tell me if that had meant anything, either. 
 Then again, something else I once read about Wittgenstein was that he used to think so hard that you could actually see him doing it. 
 And certainly I would have had no desire to put the man to that sort of trouble. 
 Wasn't that worth the update? 
 I thought so too. 
 I also upgraded this book from three stars to four. 
 By tomorrow, when I've had a full night to think on it, I may upgrade it too five. 
 UPDATE No. 2: Really, this is the very last quote I'm going to include, but I just had to include it. 
 "Men are so necessarily mad, that not to be mad would amount to another form of madness, which happens to be one more sentence that I now remember I once underlined." 
 I love that line. Just another example of the sort of narrative structure that you will either love or really hate. Yes, it's about 240 pages of that exact kind of thing. Maybe it's just that my 'inner voice' (especially when I haven't had any sleep) sounds so very much like that. Which is comforting on one hand (in that, 'oh look, I'm not the only one who thinks like that sometimes') and a bit alarming on the other hand (in the, 'oh great I must be daft then, too') sort of way. 
 What the hell, why wait til morning. Five stars it is!

I loved this book! I've been a J.R. Ward fan for years and I always worry that for some reason I won't like the newest book as much as I liked the others (my taste changes, I don't connect with the story, etc). Luckily I loved this story just as much. 
 This story includes many points of view as is the way in the Black Dagger Brotherhood series, with a focus on Trez and Selena of course. I was delighted, and kind of surprised, to get Rhage's point of view and Paradise's point of view, giving a nice lead into Blood Kiss. iAm and his lady love, which I didn't realize he'd get in this book, also experienced their own love story.  We also catch up with Xcor, Layla, and more. I'll admit that normally there is a story line that I get more excited about than the others in the book (besides the main couple) and I want to flip through the book and just follow that line and come back to the rest of the book after I've been satisfied. Though I don't do this, that's not how it was meant to be read after all, I usually have to suppress the urge to do so. Not in this book. I loved all of the story lines equally this time around. I wanted to know what was going on with everyone and how it'd pan out so much that I didn't feel the urge to do that skip. I'd get there. 
 I will admit that the ending isn't traditional for romance, but don't let that stop you from reading.  While it's not a traditional, the couple is together and mated, the ending made sense and it was a strong love story, made stronger by the fact that Selena's time was limited. I don't know if there would have been enough conflict and emotion to keep their love story as engaging without that ax hanging over their heads. And J.R. Ward doesn't leave us hanging. While there is grief, there is also an amazing show of everyone coming together. It was uplifting to get a reminder that they're more than just a band of warriors. They're a family and they take care of each other. They really do. On Trez's part there is also acceptance and a form of happiness. While I don't wish death upon any of the characters I was happy and satisfied with this ending. It was handled well and left me waiting impatiently for the next book. I couldn't ask for more than that  
 Overall, this was another great book added to the series. If you love the Black Dagger Brotherhood then this is a must buy and a must read. If you're new to the series, go pick up Dark Lover and catch up. It's a series full fighting, loving, and great world building. Just like Earth, the world of the Black Dagger Brotherhood is forever changing and along with an amazing love story you will get a world that feels real and engaging.

I mean if I was Vivian's age I think mine would have made me go with them - it is kind of like church, they go, you go but maybe I am just crazy too... who knows. 
 Anywho, on with the review - Vivian Apple suddenly finds herself without her parents in a post-rapture world. She doesn't know what to do, where they are, and she wants answers. After a few false steps, Vivian finds herself on a journey to the cult leaders secret compound to find out the true about her parents and the rapture and what she finds is SO not what she expects. 
 Vivian, the main character, was a good one. She starts as this shy wallflower and emerges into this take-charge, taking names girl in the post-apocalypse. She was interesting and I enjoyed her tale but I was more excited about her diverse best friend Harp, who used to be the take charge and slowly disintegrated in the aftermath. I found her to be a stronger character - she had a lot of influence - and she wasn't white - so rare in YA. Loved it. Then there is Peter, he seemed good enough in this book but I wasn't swooning... 
 Overall I thought this was a cool take on this what-if scenario. I think these teens acted accordingly given the situation and I think the book was good - but like I said through it all I kept thinking 'my parents would have made me...'

"Revenge. 
 I raced to finance it. 
 I evaded to protect it.

 I planned everything." 
 Dirty Ties is a "can't put down", "what the hell is happening here", "did that just really happen?" kind of read. It is action packed and full of intrigue and suspense. To anyone who enjoys some grit and rawness to their love stories, this is the perfect read for you! 
 Kaci is an independent, sophisticated, hard working business woman. She is married to her best friend and her life has been preordained to follow the lead of her parents and her husbands parents. Although she appears to have it all, on the inside she is dying a slow death. Only living for the day that she can break free! Although she loves her husband (as he is her best friend), she is truly alone. The only passion that drives her is a mystery motorcyclist that she has never met. She knows it is dangerous to want him. And yet, for some reason she is drawn to this mysterious man. 
 "A marriage that left me yearning, night after night, for an intimate connection that couldn't be sated. God, I longed for a connection that was given, not bought, despite the risks. The kind of breathless intoxication I fantasized about with a faceless man on a sportbike and had no hope of obtaining." 
 The Evader (Logan) lives a dangerous life as he races through the bustling manhattan streets. He cannot be beat. He has only one friend that assists him on his mission. What he wants is put in jeopardy when he meets Kaci. He is drawn to her. 
 "She stood out like a sparkling jewel amidst the cesspool of thugs , gangsters, and bikers who arrived in groups. She came alone, watching the finish line from the seat of her flashy pasta rocket." 
 As soon as Logan and Kaci meet, sparks are flying. However, when Logan realizes who Kaci is, he flees from her. Kaci's heart is ripped open once again. 
 "A lump crept into my throat as I fumbled for the helmet. When I found it, I shoved it on and climbed to my feet, righting my pants. Had I done something to piss him off?" 
 I simply cannot reveal any more of the story line because I just don't want to ruin it for you. I will say that I admired our heroine and hero for their determination to overcome the adversities they have been forced to face. This is a love story. It isn't full of roses and chocolates and "insta love". It is deep. It is painful. It is beautiful! Logan vows to be everything for Kaci. 
 Overall, I guess you can tell that I loved this book. The plot was well developed, the characters are extremely likable and the best part of this book is the ending. It left me satisfied and yet the story could continue. Please Ms. Godwin we want more Logan and Kaci!
