Audibook this time, which is probably the most disappointing thing about my experience with the book. I really would have wanted to go back through a couple passages and read in all the words, making up the images in my mind and sitting in vivid Africa for a while. Instead I was driving through uncomfortably muggy England with some moments of not complete focus. 
 Despite that, it's still great. It approaches a lot of new ground that I've not read about before and it does it in a way that makes it easy for the reader to approach. It won't teach you about a full and authentic experience of African life, but it gives you enough to work with and informs you of the important things. I know more about Patrice Lamumba than I ever thought I would, I know more about African food and language than I ever thought I would, and I am absolutely certain that driver ants are fucking horrifying and oh, jesus christ, I never want to be near them. 
 But there's a story under all that and it's a great one. The central characters are strong and well defined, the prose flicks between stark and truthful to flowery and picturesque, and even though there's no major antagonist or particular set piece the plot has this feeling that it's always moving forward, the characters are always trying their best to survive, and something is always happening. 
 Oh, and something that I've really got to mention is the approach to point of view and character voice. There's five perspectives that we hear from in this book, all from the first person, and I don't think I've read anything that even comes close to defining the characters so well simply by their prose. You could give me five different sentences from this book with no context and I like to think I'd have a good chance of identifying who said it. I'd get in the car after work or in the morning and turn the book back on and, nine times out of ten, even with no mention of characters or unique circumstances, I would know who was talking. It's impressive enough that it makes me a bit mad to think about it. 
 Probably the only bit that I wasn't fully sold on was the epilogue/final chapters. Following up with everyone post Africa/post Kilanga works, but feels like maybe a little overlong and ends up dispelling a lot of the tension and personality when it hops from years to years.  That being said, that dip was maybe a single 7/10 section in a 10/10 book, so it's hardly a reason not to read it.

I finished this a couple days ago (and the next three in the series) and I'm still having a hard time putting my reaction into words. As my teen daughter would say, the feels are just too big. So I'm going to do my best on this one and hope it applies to the series as a whole as much as to this specific book and keep it relatively general (because there's no way I'll be able to do this for every book in the series and I don't plan on being so detailed in future volumes). 
 While the book is structured as a mystery, that's actually the weakest aspect of the novel. It's not that hard to piece the whodunit together and really, I find that I don't much care. About the mystery. What makes the book stand-out fantastic is the characters and relationships. And I don't just mean the main characters, though that's the best part. 
 Clare is an Episcopalian priest in a small town in the Adirondacks. She is warm, kind, active, and caring in a way that true Christians strive to be. Which would make her cloying if she weren't so honestly and perfectly human at the same time. The members of her congregation are all fully-developed, complex people of faith as well with a realistic (in my experience, anyway) mixture of kind and venal, saints and hypocrites working together (often in a single person), sometimes overcoming their basest instincts and sometimes not. This book would stand out as one of the best depictions of an honest Christian community even if it never got to the second part of what makes it so awesome. 
 Russ is the chief of police in this small town. He's a true and honest servant of his people, working to keep peace in a town fallen on hard times and with a hearty mixture of the desperate and the priveleged--a potentially explosive combination. He has integrity in spades and an honest devotion to the law and doing what's right. He's also heavily married. 
 Clare and Russ are the highlight of the book as their relationship grows from honest trust and respect (with minor, uh, and major, bumps along the way) to something... more. By the end, it is absolutely heartbreaking as Russ and Clare become aware of what the reader has suspected for some time--that they are perfectly matched, almost made for each other and that they have no way of doing anything about it without breaking both of them into something less than they are now. The poignancy of this is heartbreaking in its tragedy and purity and humanity. 
 Which makes it seem like the book would be heavy. But that's the genius of Julia Spencer-Fleming--she manages to pull off that powerful emotional impact without losing the hope that lies at the heart of faith and integrity. It is easy to forget that Christianity is, at heart, a faith for the fallen and that its promise isn't ease or success or protection from harm but rather comfort in affliction and the eventual achievement of grace. Infusing a hint of grace into the promise of heartbreak (and making both real and powerful) is an amazing achievement and I am so happy to have found it in this story.

 While cleaning the streets during detention, Cadence met Mark Connelly. When she came back to school, she discovered that he is her math teacher. They fell in love and entered in a secret relationship (which includes a sexual relationship). 
 Good also showed Cadence's point of view on Christianity, and how she interpreted the Word of God, and how she let it affect her decisions and her relationship with Mark who has different beliefs compared to hers. This also twisted her beliefs in some way. In some parts of the story, I saw that instead of her Christian beliefs affecting her relationship, it was her relationship that affected her beliefs.

3.0 stars, maybe just below. 
 This book is an okay book and a quick read. The story and the world is fairly original and interesting; a good premise. The characters are hit and miss. Some of the children seem kind of interesting, but many of the other characters are very flat and undeveloped. Overall, I recommend this book for anyone who enjoys typical YA fantasy novels. I wouldn't say it is anything explosively amazing, but it's an okay book to pass the time and some other people seemed to have really enjoyed it. 
 My issues with this book is that though the world, the peculiar children and the loops are all interesting and pretty original, the story isn't really. It is a very typical story. Bad guys vs good guys and where the main character thinks the world is totally normal and then finds out it's not really. Main character then decides to team up with the good guys to fight the good fight. The bad guys are quite obviously and directly bad. There is no depth to their madness. They are not misunderstood, nor have they fallen off some righteous path. They are by the book bad guys (and so, of course, they are allied with the token historical straightforward bad guys: Nazis). The good guys are not only pretty typical 'we just want to be free to live in peace' good guys and they have the added element of being innocent children. On that note though, why would they still mentally be children? If their timeline is continuous, then shouldn't their stream of consciousness be developing into adulthood even if their bodies aren't? I mean you could argue their brains are limited physically and so they still have kid brains, but by that argument their synapses (as being part of their physical selves) would also be restored at the changeover meaning all new memories would be forgotten and therefore no continuous stream of consciousness could be established. Major plot hole. 
 Aside from this, another major factor in the story is that huge disaster could have been avoided if things were just communicated earlier. This is something that is really way overdone in YA literature and is very annoying as a reader. In this book it was Miss. Peregrine saying that Jake needed to say immediately if anything out of the ordinary was happening that could be a sign of creature that eat people. The same kind of creature who killed his grandfather, whose murder was blamed on a pack of dogs. Yet, for some unfathomable reason, the group of sheep that had just recently been torn up in the exact same manner and the strange newcomer who orders raw meat doesn't seem to warrant any mention.  
 In general, this book seems like it is trying to mimic a John Green novel and throw in some fantasy. It doesn't come together so well. It is a quick read to pass the time, but it is not extraordinary. In fact, it is super ordinary. I will not continue with the books.

Aaaaaah look, overall, this book delivered what I'd expected. It surprised me in a few places, skirting around issues that I thought it'd have (the love cures mental illness trope) with ease, and delighted me in others (the family!!). But it never really came together in the way it sort of promised it might... 
 I was very worried, going into this, that it was going to be one of those "girl has genuine problems until her love for a new boy solves everything" books. You know, that super relatable and realistic story that's not even a little infuriating... And of course, the whole premise of this book does set it up a little unavoidably, so I was aware that I was going to cringe a little. In the end, I only picked it up because I kept seeing it at the library and remembering all the good reviews. I guess they weren't for nothing. 
 The problem was the romance itself. Because its like we were given a few corner pieces of a puzzle and then expected to believe that suddenly that was an entire picture. (I feel like that simile got away from me in the middle there, but it's the best way I can word it right now) The characters weren't bad? Linus was a sweet outline of a character, and Audrey was relatable (well okay to fourteen year old me, and also anxiety/lizard brain me but.... still points), but there was no chemistry. Or at least, no on page chemistry. 
 I mean, don't get me wrong I thought the notes were cute, and the nicknames and the games... but there's not really any reason for Linus to care so much. I could understand curiosity, but he has a crush without any real motivation for one, given that their talking is limited quite severely. He only met her once before, so it's not even like he remembers who she is outside of the anxiety. I guess it's just you're not shown what would make this random teenage boy be anything more than just polite to his best friend's sister, especially given that she runs and hides every time he comes near at first. 
 And then later we're expected to believe they're in love?? I mean obviously we're talking high school love, but still... they keep talking about all these texts and these hang outs... but all we're shown are these challenges. Don't get me wrong, they're super cute! I just find it hard to take it from quirky dares to somehow they know and trust each other so much....  
 This would have bugged me a lot more, if not for the fact that Audrey's family takes up so much of the book. Felix was honestly such a gift of a character. Having a much younger brother myself, I could relate so much to the kinda shift in dynamics with an age gap like that, and the antics of little kids. Honestly his contributions were so spot on, and so funny. He reminded me a lot of my little brother.... maybe that's why I'm so soft on him. 
 Audrey's parents were a little over the top... but I found it more funny than annoying. I think I really appreciate antics in a book (like the argument with the siblings over Shreddies, and the mum's obsession with daily mail and everything that caused). It adds a lot of life to the book and, though it's kinda exaggerated to make it interesting, it hits a little closer to the truth. That sort of chaos is what families are like, or at least what my experience of them has been like (especially ones with lots of kids ahaha) . 
 The final thing that I really enjoyed about this book was the portrayal of anxiety. What I liked most was those ups, amidst the downs, because that is something often missed by authors writing about anxiety. It's too easy to write panic on edge all the time, but that's not what it's like. There's periods of it going away, and you thinking its gone, and then it can come back in manageable ways and overwhelming ways, and it's not often that books really show all of this at once.  I also liked the sort of techniques she used, and the relationship she had with her counsellor. Well, save the whole going off her meds thing. But that was also another really well done plot, because I feel like that feeling good and stopping medication is so common, and that delay between her choice and the consequences was crucial.  
 I feel like I would have enjoyed this book more if I'd just had more?? More details, more feelings, I guess? I'm not sure. It wasn't a a bad book, though. A good thing to read between assignments to clear my head a little...

 Much of what I said for the first book, 
 Slated 
 [review], still applies to 
 Fractured 
 - Kyla is still this intriguing little enigma of a person, and the book is still compulsively readable, with a very skin-crawlingly plausible (as an extreme) basis for a dystopia. As the series goes on and the reader is given more information and more of an insight into what's really happening, everything gets a little darker and more worrisome in a really interesting way. The more that is revealed, the more questions there are to ask. 
 I love the layers Teri Terry has presented in this story. There is intrigue, terrorism and patriotism, politics and science and double-crosses, all muddled up together into a full, tension-fraught, scarily real world. These elements play off of each other, each heightening the next and creating more tension and anticipation for what is to come - there are so many places things can start to go wrong, and the reasons things have come to this extreme are both horrifyingly believable and just-enough over the edge as to be almost too much. Kyla is an excellent representation of all of this; she is all these different people, stacked one in another like matryoshka. She's naive and innocent, but also strong, smart and uncanny. She's incredibly vulnerable and broken, but fierce and seemingly unbreakable. The things that have been done to her - and not just the Slating, but the layers and layers of things, which are hinted at in book 1 and explored more in book 2 - have created in Kyla quite an enigma, which doesn't quite fit anywhere, but has pieces of every aspect of this intricate world reflected in her. 
 The more Kyla understands about her world and herself, the more intriguing and dangerous everything becomes, and I love it! Of course, it helps that Terry's writing pulls you along at high speed. As with Slated, I Didn't intend to read this in a day, but I damn near did. Terry just makes it so easy to keep flipping pages; I had to know what Kyla was going to remember next, or how she was going to get out of every predicament. As the series progresses, new characters pop into Kyla's life with greater frequency, and who they are and their motivations are always suspect. With each new interaction, the stakes are raised, and you're left constantly wondering how things could possibly end well. And the beauty of the book? 
 Sometimes they don't. 
 That may sound strange to you, but think about what a beautiful thing that is, to not have everything clean and nice and tied up with a bow. Life isn't always clean and nice; life is hard. Sometimes things suck. Sometimes good people get hurt and bad ones keep on doing the hurting, and very little adds up or makes sense or feels right. That's life. In a dystopian society? It should be just that, but more. Things should be heightened, danger should be real, and it should feel as though maybe there just isn't a Happily Ever After. That's the only way I can really buy in, and I'm so glad that Teri Terry gets* that and doesn't cop out and wave a magic wand so that everyone comes out unscathed and perfect**, happy and whole. I appreciate that so much. 
 I appreciate the danger and the questions and the tension, and just GAH! is it time for book 3 yet?!

 My Thoughts: 
 No Angel is not a book that I would typically pick up and read because I tend to shy away from books that attempt humor. I was sent a review copy randomly by Harper Teen and was actually pleasantly surprised with how enjoyable this was. Keeble's writing is not overly serious; this book is pure fun and was a quick and easy read. 
 I really enjoyed that No Angel moved at a fast pace and was told from a male point of view. I felt Keeble did a great job in giving Raffi a distinctive and masculine tone. He was incredibly likeable and some of his lines were very, very funny. My favorite parts were his development of his angel gifts. I felt the writing was very descriptive and did a wonderful job with the physical comedy of the situations Raffi found himself in. 
 The secondary cast was written well though I was never overly connected to them or really understood all their motivations. Some of the characters felt disjointed in their development, though it didn't really detract from my overall enjoyment. 
 Though aspects were done beautifully my biggest issue with the main story arc was its predictability. The twists were never surprising to me and I never felt overly engaged in the outcome. 
 Final Thoughts: 
 No Angel was an entertaining book that was a bit of a fluff read. I would read another Helen Keeble book without a doubt because her writing was easy, fun and a humorous take on paranormal young adult fiction.

"What if Shakespeare has it wrong? What if the right question is not to be but how to be?" 
 I was not aware that Gayle Forman has a new book until it was released and I really wanted to smack myself for it. I am a huge fan of her If I Stay series and yes, I will read anything she writes. So when I had my copy of Just One Day, I started right off not knowing what the story is about. And once again, Forman delivered. 
 Just One Day lived up to its title since the story revolved around that one day when Allyson and Willem met and fell in love. How that one day changed Allyson's life since. Okay, I have to admit, I am NOT so crazy over instant love in books. I don't like them BUT Forman's writing is so beautiful and I was really captivated so I let go of my prejudices and embraced the story and just loved it so. 
 Basically, the story is about this girl, Allyson on a trip in Europe. She is the kind of girl who let the world see a different girl from the outside. She does what she's supposed to. It's like her true self is trapped inside a box where she can't get out. She pretends she wants to go to premed because that's what her parents want her to do. She pretends to enjoy the trip when the truth is it just bores her. And so on. Then, she met Willem. He offered to take her to Paris for one day. Not knowing that one day will truly change her and the one thing in her life she won't be able to forget. Ever. He brought her out of the box. He brought out the 'Lulu' in her and she loved it. They fell in love. They were "stained". (Stained: being in love) 
 Then, Willem was gone. Lulu became Allyson again. Year later, Allyson could not still move on. It was like a huge part of her was left in Paris. So, she decided to go back to seek for answers about why he left her... 
 But I think that it's not only about Willem. It's also about Allyson wanting to find that girl she once became when she was in Paris. The carefree girl who had fun, and did stuff Allyson would never do. Like, say, throw a book to scary guys to save Willem. So her journey back to Paris is discovering how she can be that girl again. How to be.... 
 I really, really need that second book right now. And the fact that it's in Willem's POV drives me crazy. How can I wait any longer after that ending, Miss Gayle Forman? Tell me? So, once again, another wonderful story that blew me away. 
 "Now tell me how long you would have her after you have possessed her." 
 "For ever and a day." 
 (P.S. I have a very important question. This really kept me up last night. Is Willem a vampire? He DID lick her blood from his finger, mind you! Okay, I'm done.)
A bit lighter than I wanted it to be, but it is always fun to hang with Charley and the gang!

I hadn't heard of this book before seeing it on our library's list of popular ebooks, but it looked very intriguing, so I checked it out. Reading it on my small little iPhone screen probably wasn't ideal for getting the best effect from the photographs, but I really didn't mind. It made me pay closer attention to the story, which I think was a good thing. 
 The writing is done well. I liked how real all of the characters and their interactions seemed. The author didn't seem to waste any opportunity for meaning or depth, and it made me relate to and ache for more people than just the main character, even if they were only featured for just a short amount of time. Strangely, the peculiar children come off a bit flatter than the regular-world ones do - not quite as much depth yet. But there are possible reasons for this, and I hope Riggs fixes that in the subsequent books. 
 The pictures were a nice touch, but I have to say that I'm glad I read the book not knowing that they were real. It made them less obtrusive, and it interrupted my immersion in the story less. I recommend reading this book thinking of the photos as a footnote and taking the time to marvel at them later. Otherwise it is easy for the story to start to feel contrived to fit in the photos instead of the photos fitting the story. 
 There are a few unanswered questions that nag at me a bit (How did Victor die? If they exited the loop in the past, then wouldn't they see his grandfather leaving the island at the same time too? ), but all in all it was a good read and an intriguing look at antique photographs.

 Continuing the big "Echelon" story arc from The Doomsday Key and The Devil Colony, the True Bloodline at the very heart of the dreaded international terror group known as the Guild has been revealed to Sigma Force Director Painter Crowe. It's the family of sitting US President James T. Gant. At the end of the last novel, it appeared that the Gant family, including the President himself, was secretly evil. And, in between the usual historical prologue and Part 1, there is a brief section, taking place on the Fourth of July (five days after the major action starts), in which Gray Pierce appears to assassinate the President. At first, I was happy to see this, because I thought that Sigma had commanded Pierce to eliminate a corrupt leader. But there is much more to the story. 
 Out on the high seas, the President's daughter, Amanda Gant-Bennett, has been kidnapped by Somali pirates. But these are no ordinary pirates. They are led by a white British doctor. And the doctor wants her unborn baby son, because the son has a very unusual genetic mutation - triple-helical DNA. According to this doctor, the third helix holds the key to a popular human wish - immortality. 
 Reluctantly, Director Crowe sends out Pierce, Seichan, and Kowalski to rescue the First Daughter, along with former MP Tucker Wayne and his fearsome (and stolen) military dog, Kane. As you can expect, they kick ass and take names. Back home, Kat Bryant is sent to Charleston, SC, to the fertility clinic where Amanda was impregnated with her test-tube baby. What does all this mean? And more importantly, is the President part of the Guild/Echelon conspiracy? Or is he just an unwitting pawn? 
 The answers, I cannot reveal. But I will say that it is perhaps the most insane scheme Sigma has yet been forced to contend with, as the True Bloodline proves seemingly unstoppable. The mission is so intense, they're forced to call Monk Kokkalis out of retirement, and to call on the services of Lisa Cummings' ex, Jack Kirkland (who you might remember if you've read Deep Fathom.) The identity of Seichan's father is revealed, and it's pretty shocking. And then there's the ending, which is possibly the most awesome, holy-crap-what-did-that-guy-just-do karmic ending you'll ever see.  
 You will be shocked and awed by this novel, and not just by Sigma's operation which was classified as such by the President.

FIRST OF ALL: Let me just say that so much wrong can be said about this. The ending. The sudden changes. The world-building flaws. The unanswered questions. The inconsistencies. ADAM. But to be honest, none of those things really outweighed the fact that this book was pretty darn awesome. 
 Because it was. Pretty darn awesome, I mean. ;) 
 The winner for me in this is obvious: Warner. I have always been Team Warner even when there wasn't really anything but a Team Adam, mostly because I'm a sucker for the evil types (the Darkling, Death, Varen, etc.), but also because I feel like his character was the most fleshed out. Whereas Tahereh Mafi (bless her creative soul [?]) didn't really dive much into Adam or Kenji or even Juliette's messed up pasts, she always made sure that her readers had a clear understanding of Aaron Warner Anderson. How can you NOT love him, knowing what you do? Especially after the scene with his mother! :'(  
 Also: Kenji? I mean, COME ON. He literally was my saving grace in this book! [?] He's Juliette's best friend, the voice of only reason at the funniest times, and laugh-out-loud funny as the comic relief with his hilarious sarcastic comments! I want him as my best friend too! 
 I always have some trouble with Tahereh's writing though -- not because of the originality of Juliette's mind fragments (which I love) but because of how inconsistent it was. That was especially evident in this installment. Maybe it was because Juliette grows so much as a character in this book (less afraid, more confident, and a million times more epic!), or maybe because clear writing was the only way to progress the plot without extending this book past a thousand pages, but the excessive metaphors and incoherency was almost completely absent! I don't know if that's a good thing or not yet. I just know that I really, really noticed. 
 I'm literally writing this review on my phone at two o'clock in the morning before my first day back at school after exams (because I'm just that smart LOL), but I had to say this: I LOVED this installment! It was stronger, more plot-focused, and less of an emotional mess. It was totally risky and it totally paid off, because it was nothing short of brilliant. :) 
 I can't wait to see what Tahereh works on next!

 I'm feeling pretty middle-of-the road about this book. It's clearly one of the author's first attempts at writing a mystery, and she does pretty well at it. I think where this book fails is that Gerritsen doesn't chose a POV character. She switches back and forth between Catherine Cordell, the unsub, Detective Moore, and Detective Rizzoli. This ends up hurting her because she doesn't give Rizzoli enough focus early in the book for me to buy it when she wraps up the mystery from her point of view. She focuses too much on Moore, who apparently doesn't feature heavily in the rest of the books in this series. Catherine Cordell's narrative could have been interesting if she'd been more heavily involved in the case, but for most of the book she refuses to have anything but the bare minimum to do with it, then suddenly she's in love with Moore and heavily invested. The unsub's sections could have been dropped altogether without hurting the plot. I've never been a big fan of dropping first-person narrative from the culprit into the middle of third-person narratives. I also thought that Gerritsen hurt herself by not introducing us to the unsub from one of our other POV characters' perspectives. Catherine at least could have run into him. It would have made the conclusion more personal and more engaging had that been the case. 
 There were a few places where Gerritsen made me uncomfortable with her terminology. For instance, the Surgeon of the title, a serial killer, targets rape victims. A lot of the words used to describe the victims is now considered improper or archaic. The killer also cuts out the victim's uterus to "purify" her. Instead of referring to the uterus by it's proper, scientific name, everyone in the book, from the doctors right on down to the killer himself, calls it "the womb." The entire book, it's "He cut out her womb" and "he was holding the womb." It got annoying and a little insulting after a while. It also seemed very unprofessional coming from a doctor. There was also a ton of victim-shaming. 
 Jane Rizzoli herself was actually quite unpleasant. I think she's supposed to be inexperienced and trying to prove herself in a man's world, but she just came off annoying, bitchy, and mean. She also appeared to be a man-hater, due to her actions toward pretty much every man she meets, even the ones who don't question her authority on the force. And when Moore does the honorable, truthful, logical thing and doesn't lie about whether or not a man she shoots has a gun, she gets so upset and angry that she tells on him for having what at that point was a pretty harmless affair with a victim. And calls him a traitor to his face, despite his being one of the few men who actually treats her no different than anyone else on the force. Rizzoli also has a dangerously unhealthy attitude about herself and her looks. Quite honestly, I understood her meanness and her previously inexplicably self-destructive behavior a lot better and with a lot more sympathy when I realized was supposed to be because she hated herself most of all. 
 All of that being said, The Surgeon was a fast, entertaining read. Gerritsen assumes her reader is smart enough to catch most of the more common technical lingo (both in the medical world and the police department) or to have context for it from other places. She defines or explains her more uncommon terms (CODIS, for example) but assumes her readers will be familiar enough with the jargon not to need her to explain everything she says. The plot was also very quickly-paced, and felt pretty well thought out as far as the big picture. I found it all quite enjoyable despite it's flaws, so I'm interested to see if Gerritsen improves as she goes. I'll probably pick up the next book in the series soon.

I was initially a bit skeptical about the journal-style format of the book, but after the first chapter, I was hooked. Absolutely amazing story. There were many moments throughout the book where I either whooped for joy, or screamed in frustration. Any book that can elicit such sounds is a winner in my book. Not only that, but the book was just outright funny at times, and you find yourself rooting for Mark Watney from page one. If I were to have one criticism of the book, it would be that the dialogue, at times, seemed rather clunky and unrealistic. I understand that Andy Weir needed to explain the science in layman's terms, but I doubt that when two astrophysicists converse, one would say something complicated, and the other would re-iterate it in simpler terms. The other astrophysicist would know what the first meant in said complicated terms. Nothing major, and it didn't detract from the story; just a minor complaint. Other than that, it was the best book I have read all year. Couldn't recommend it enough.

I can pinpoint the exact moment in this work where it went from being a "good" read into being an "ok" one--when King essentially states that improving one's writing is hopeless unless you happen to fall in the category of being a "competent writer." According to King, writers fall into four categories: the bad, the competent, the good, and the great. And apparently, bad writers can never become competent and good writers will never become great. Hogwash. I don't know if I've ever used this term before, but you've forced it out of me, Mr. King. Moving beyond this sticking point, I will say I found the autobiographical parts of this book to be interesting (you can't deny he's a character). Some of his tips for writing are useful, albeit not groundbreaking, but others, such as those mentioned above, I take issue with. It's worth a read, but take some of his advice with a grain of salt.

I wasn't super excited that The Program had a sequel, but since I enjoyed that book so much I wanted to check out The Treatment, and honestly I wasn't really impressed. Nothing really happened, in my opinion. At least other than pointless love triangles. 
 Admittedly, I had trouble recalling what happened in The Program, and looking back at my other review I see why. But I definitely remember enjoying that book a lot more than this one. And thinking it really didn't need a sequel. It just bugs me that Sloane has flat out told Realm that she doesn't love him, she considers him a friend and he doesn't back off and he keeps trying to make a move when Sloan is clearly in a happy relationship with James. It bothers me that Dallas is used as some sort of way to put a wedge between Sloane and James when she and Sloane could have worked very well together. I mean you're in the middle of some sort of rebellion or revolution here, I think the least of your problems should be who you are dating. 
 On that note, the "rebels" were really just a handful of kids who didn't know what they were doing. I'm surprised they lasted as long as they did. But in the end, they weren't really the ones to take down the organization. So what was their point? They didn't even contribute a lot to the ultimate take down of The Program. Dallas turned into a crazy mess (rightfully so, I have no objections to her character other than using her to put a wedge between Sloane and James), Lacey was useless in the end, Realm was a dick, Cas a traitor, and Sloane and James really just wanted to run off by themselves and try to live happily ever after. I mean, good for them, but there's just a few more important things to deal with first. 
 I don't know, I just really don't think this was needed. I think if the first one was tweaked a bit, and ended differently, it would have been a great standalone novel. So really, this wasn't needed, but it also could have been executed better. Nothing important really happened until the last couple chapters, and it made everything feel rushed. I'm not really looking forward to the novellas, but I will check them out if I get the chance, just because I think they deserve a chance.

This book seemingly has all of the marks of a good novel. 
 Epicly powerful, scarily horrific antagonist? Check. 
 Powerful protagonist who is already loved from previous stories and has known power? Check. 
 Conflict over the fate of the universe? Check. 
 Evil character who's deliciously unsure of himself? Check. 
 Satisfying plot? Che-- Wait, I'm lying. This book had beautiful characters created by an author who has no concept of how to link them together, what emotional bonds should be stressed, and how to not totally piss a reader off. 
 From now on, there will be massive spoilers. 
 First, we have a book based on a universe in which approximately twenty support characters have already been created for this time period. In this book, we see three of them. Firstly, this is unacceptable because I find it highly unlikely that these characters would part from Revan, and with their skill set I find it equally unlikely that Revan would not ask for their help. 
 Second, it comes to light that-- according to this author, who I am pointedly choosing to disbelieve-- Revan and Malak became evil only because they were forced to by someone so powerful they couldn't control themselves, which is utterly obnoxious. So you're basically taking a series which has been argued to have one of the best plotlines of any videogame and reducing the motivations of the main character to mind control? Great job ruining any respect one could ever have for said characters. 
 Finally, the ending. Oh, the ending. It was atrocious. It was obnoxious. It was unbelievable. And frankly, it wasn't an ending. Without another book to tie off the plotline that has been created, this book doesn't have it's own end. I have to wonder if Karpyshyn chose to do this specifically so that he could have another book deal to make money off of, because no author worth their salt would ever write a non-ending such as this. The Twilight Series had better closure.

 I'm not giving it five stars because, like I said, I hated Nick and Amy. By the end, I didn't hate Nick anymore. I didn't hate him too much anyway, despite his personal flaws I don't even dislike him for being a cheater, considering the type of person his wife was , so I wanted him to beat this and come out on top. I was rooting for him. I still didn't particularly like him, but I didn't hate him anymore. 
 Amy. I hate Amy. Amy is a bitch. A crazy psycho bitch. No justice there! She didn't get punished! She won! I didn't want her to win! If she wasn't going to die, I wanted her to be made contrite! It didn't happen! God! I hate her!  
 The initial twist, I was expecting. Almost everything that happened after that, I did not expect and I was honestly hooked. I'd have finished this book much sooner if not for that cruise I went on and the time spent trying to get back into the flow of things once the vacation was over. 
 The ending threw me. Another reason I can't give this five stars. Mostly, because it wasn't what I wanted. I admire Flynn for ending it that way. Much different from how books like this tend to end. Spoiler!: She gets away with it!  
 Still, the book made me rage. I can't believe the way things played out. I wanted to kill a bitch or at least kick her in the throat. 
 I don't truly understand how I don't hate this book, but also not like it. It did make me feel strong emotions. But they were basically all negative. I didn't like these people. She could have given me at least one person to like, right? 
 What a ride this book was.

Probably the best the urban fantasy genre has to offer. That may seem like damning with faint praise, considering the competition, but Night Watch really does stand head and shoulders above them. 
 Bromfield's translation is imperfect and unwieldy, and Lukyanenko's views on morality are pathologically Russian, but the former adds to the atmosphere that makes the latter easy to disregard. As is usual for the genre, there are a fair number of plot holes, some of them glaringly obvious, but the setting is interesting enough that they don't significantly affect your enjoyment of the stories. 
 Every reviewer ends up comparing the books to the movies, but this is one of those rare instances where watching the movies actually makes the book more enjoyable, especially if you aren't too concerned about strictly delimiting canon.

Really, really enjoyed this. I opted for the Audiobook because the author had some very good things to say about it and i have to agree. R.C. Bray does an excellent job of narrating this. 
 I decided to read it after i heard the author being interviewed on a podcast (Treks in Sci-Fi). I was fascinated by the story behind how this little self published novel came to be a great word of mouth hit which was eventually picked up by a publisher and i noted with some interest was being sold on the shelves in my local supermarket today and is a planned 2015 movie to be directed by Ridley Scott. 
 I think i loved this for 2 very different reasons. 
 Firstly it is by far at its best when we are 1:1 with the main character, Mark Watney. Much of the book is in his voice as he narrates his daily log and as such how much you like this book is going to be contingent on how much you like the main character because like Tom Hanks in Castaway (which is an obvious influence) you get to spend an awful lot of time with him, sharing his triumphs and disasters but more importantly his sense of humour. 
 Secondly the elements where others are brought into the narrative, sometimes in parallel to Mark's trials and tribulation and in other times in flashback are a little less successful but still work well enough to keep the narrative moving. I did initially find it a little jarring when we moved from the format of Mark directly recording his daily log to other characters having real time conversations with each other but this soon wore off. I soon began to enjoy this for its obvious Apollo 13'ishness plus it was also reminiscent of the Sci-Fi disaster/action fiction of Harry Harrison who is one of my favourite authors. 
 I also think it is a testament to the skill of the author that a book so packed with technical and scientific detail, (1) didn't leave me cold or (2) didn't have me banging my fist on the table annoyed because something or other just didn't make sense. I was so swept away by the narrative that i just didn't worry about any of that. 
 Read this novel because this first time author is a great discovery and it's always great when someone decides to have a go, with no real expectation and it gets noticed. Read it because it's going to be made into a massive Sci-Fi film. But mainly read it because it is bloody good!

While Fateful was a good book, it is also a book of cliches and simplicity. Tess is a servant who is dreaming of a better life. Alex is a young man who's brooding about his curse and is basically, willing to lead a lonely existence if it means he won't hurt anyone. Sound familiar? 
 A servant dreaming of a better life is nothing new, neither is a young man whose depressed and wants to love a girl, but can't because he's dangerous. Fateful is a very simple story. For example, the part about a werewolf brotherhood was very watered down. There's nothing about how the Brotherhood came about, how they got their magic, details, details, details. There's nothing. 
 The romance was very instant. Tess meets Alex and all of a sudden, they're in love. I understand how they might fall in love, Alex being lonely and Tess seeking companionship outside of her lowly servant life. But really, it was a little eyeball-rolling worthy. Especially the part of them having sex for the first time, and Tess apparently says that it didn't hurt because she loved him. Really? How rough is the werewolf curse if he's able to control it enough to have sex with her?  
 The lead-up to the sinking was good. Tess' emotions were really powerful; about how she realized that there weren't enough lifeboats and how so many people were going to die. I was so sad that all those characters we knew were probably going to die. But then it was over. Tess is knocked unconscious and then, suddenly, we're out of the ship and BOOM, it's done! 
 I was, however, really sad when I learned about the deaths of Miss Irene and Ned. They were probably the only other couple I was actually interested in, and to learn of their forbidden romance, and the fact they couldn't really have a life together in life was just heartbreaking. I was so of sad that they died but at least they got to be together.  
 The ending was super convenient too. I mean, really. Overall, Fateful is not a bad book, but it could have been a lot better. I felt that the author was trying to squeeze everything into 328 pages and that simply wasn't enough.

A major complaint that I'm seeing in the reviews for this book is how slowly the plot moves. And those reviewers have a point. The plot is largely nonexistent for most of the book. 
 But The Graces isn't a plot-driven book. It's all about character. Specifically, the characters Fenrin, Thallia, and Summer Grace and their relationship with our mysterious, unlikable narrator, River. Spoilers, it's not a healthy relationship. 
 So yes, there's very little in the way of plot. But The Graces is an evil, malicious little book, and I adore its darkness and its willingness to fully commit to its own mad desires and plans. And it's so wonderful to read a book that sets up so many tired YA cliches and then sidesteps them quite neatly. 
 It's been a while since I've read a YA book that takes risks. The Graces takes risks in leaps and bounds, and in my opinion, those risks pay off handily.

 Definitely post-apoc worth reading.

 Initial Reaction 1/18/14: This was actually a pleasant surprise!!! It was really interesting to see Charley and Thad figure out the mysteries of Nil. I was trying to figure it out the whole time and I was hooked! 
 Full review originally seen on The Book Addict's Guide 2/12/14: NIL was actually a pleasant surprise for me. I started reading not sure what to expect and I ended up really enjoying so many of the characters and their backstories as well as the mystery of the island of Nil. I was worried that the explanation of its mysteries would be cheesy because for the life of me, I could NOT figure out what was going on but I was very satisfied with the way everything played out! 
 Before I get into the details, let me tell you that my mind was racing with comparisons as I was reading -- definitely in a good way. NIL was a really interesting concept and I kept seeing several mash-ups of my favorite books and TV shows... #1 was Monument 14 meets Lost. NIL has the great action that I loved in Monument 14 and teens of all ages who are strangers working together to stay safe and survive while at the same time figuring out the mystery of a deadly island. #2 was The Maze Runner meets Gilligan's Island. The island of NIL has a lot more secrets than we first realize and I loved the comradery that the kids built. #3 was Lord of the Flies meets Survivor. The kids don't always work well together and... well... sometimes people turn on each other. 
 One of the things I loved the most about the book was the range of characters we meet. The only humans on the island of Nil are all teenagers and the "gates" that bring people to the islands collect them from all over the world. They have a lot of differences but because they're all stuck in the same odd and hostile situation, they easily band together to form a (mostly) tight group. Obviously they can't force everyone to get along so it was interesting the conflicts that arise as well as how each of their "mortality rates" (each person only has 365 days on Nil before Nil takes them (aka, they die)) affects how the group gets along. I really enjoyed the diversity of the characters, both in age range and home country. 
 The mystery of the island totally stumped me -- and that's a good thing. I really did spend the entire book trying to figure out what in the world was going on and even as the characters were collecting clues, I was still totally in the dark. The best part? It was a GOOD surprise. I think I was so worried about the book because of the way Lost ended up taking a turn. A great TV show with so many mysteries and it turned kind of weird (especially the end) so with that Lost parallel already in my head, I think that's where most of the fear came from! I wonder if Lynne Matson had been a fan of the show because she definitely didn't let her readers down and the explanation how of Nil worked was wonderful! There was one main question I don't think we ever got the answer to but not enough to really feel like I was missing something! 
 I also really appreciated the romance between Charley and Thad. Cute island boy meets cute island girl? Come on, you know that's starting a romance. I can understand where people might feel that it's kind of insta-lovey but it really didn't come off to me like that at all. There are plenty of instances where I've been in their shoes and developed a huge crush right off the bat, then the more you get to know about a person the more you love about them. NIL was totally that. Combine a strong attraction with living with someone and spending all your time with them PLUS he's your island guide and person who teaches you how to survive this crazy place? Oh, please. Giiiiirl, you are totally falling in love with him. I loved Charley & Thad's fun and easy-going relationship. They had friendly banter, healthy competition, and really just clicked. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed his book! I know I went in a little hesitant but I totally had nothing to worry about. It was a really interesting sci-fi book that really stayed in the realm of science fiction and I love that Lynne Matson didn't throw too much into the book either. I feel like the intricate workings of Nil could have easily gotten complicated and easily saturated with all kinds of science-fiction and paranormal aspects, but the explanation was unique and mostly concise and it totally worked for me!

I've been hearing about Bad Feminist for years now. I remember when it was a Goodreads Choice nominee way back in 2014. I thought, hey, I need to get my hands on that asap. Well, it's 2017 and I've finally gotten my hands on it. This book was supposed to be groundbreaking. It was advertised as "sharp" and "funny." 
 I don't know what I expected, but it wasn't this. 
 Quite honestly, reading this book was a chore. And that's saying something, really, because I am actually interested in the topics of (most of) Gay's essays. We seem to have a lot of the same views. I think that we'd probably get along if we met in real life. But, unfortunately, when it comes to connecting with a book, there are things more important than a shared worldview. 
 There's actually very little about feminism in this book. There are a number of essays about race and multiple open and honest discussions of sexual violence. Gay writes in-depth critiques of a plethora of books that I've never read and movies that I've never seen, including one "think piece" about 50 Shades in which she laments the number of "think pieces" that have already been written about it. She discusses controversial news stories and comments on various celebrities. She mentions Paula Deen in no less than three separate essays. There is an oddly detailed account of her time playing competitive Scrabble. Some of these topics are related, at least tangentially, to feminism. But many are not. This is much more of a memoir than a cohesive collection of essays on feminism. 
 I was not at all surprised to find that these essays were not written for this book. They've appeared on Gay's blog and in various online and print media. Some are well-written. Others are sloppy and rushed. I don't think an editor ran through the essays to try to tie them together or to make sure there were no glaring errors before this book went to publication. It may be because I (briefly) worked as an editor, but the inconsistency in Gay's writing really grated on me. For instance, there's one sentence where she decides to use the word "whom" and then finishes with a dangling preposition. Yes, I'm nit-picking, and no, it's not the end of the world, but while errors like that are fine on your personal blog, they don't belong in a published book. 
 I remember once, maybe five or so years ago, one of my female acquaintances told me that I couldn't call myself a feminist if I worked for a male boss in a typically female-driven field. (At the time, I was working as a receptionist for a male physician.) Setting aside any discussion of the sheer level of privilege that her job criteria might require, her overall attitude reminded me of Gay's. Without a doubt, she has good intentions. But for all of her reading about feminism and her railing against the rigid ideas of feminism that society instills in us, she too has come up with some odd ideas about what exactly a feminist should be. 
 She seems almost contrite as she admits that she prefers the color pink, that she likes pretty dresses and dreams of a large closet of shoes, that she happily reads Vogue and listens to rap music and devours mindless chick lit. This, apparently, makes her a bad feminist. I can't say that I agree. 
 I've read better and more coherent essays on feminism for free on Tumblr.

What would you do if your son was accused of murder? That's the premise of this excellent legal thriller by William Landay. 
 What I liked about this book was the knowledge of the law and psychology that the author brought to the story. For example, one moves an exhibit "in" evidence, not "into" evidence. Landay gets this bit of nuance because he knows his subject matter. The book is also current by Landay's inclusion of pop culture references and cutting edge science over the question of whether the desire to kill is tied to one's DNA and thus can be inherited. 
 My only criticism of the book is that half of the story is told during the ADA's questioning of the accused's father during a grand jury investigation. I understand and appreciate the technique. However, I think that the story would have flowed better without it. 
 Overall, I highly recommend this one and look forward to reading more by Landay.

You know when I first got to a part about iridescent green roaches running around the Teleporter Machine, a little warning bell went off in my brain. And I was trying to think of horror book I had read recently that featured them, but shrugged and kept going because its an interesting book with different but engaging hero. 
 Mike Erikson is one of the world's smartest people, with instant recall of everything he's ever seen or read, but has instead chosen a life of careful mediocrity teaching high school English rather than be a tortured genius. However, old buddy and DARPA budget comptroller begs him to be the eyes on the ground for this top-secret government project. Some scientists have built a teleporter that has run hundreds of perfect tests, but the scientists all seem a bit shifty and the news too good to be true, plus a few little accidents. 
 I was pretty far along into this before I realized oh those green bugs? Same bugs from 14, another book Cline wrote with an actual crossover at the end between the two. I LOVED 14, but in retrospect it was a bit bloated and probably 30 or so pages could have been cut that might have tightened it up a bit. (The Fold is much more of a rollicking book I think in comparison.) And like 14, it's a man investigating an intriguing mystery that starts off as odd, gets weirder and then  one minute you're looking at info on the computer and a few hours later racing across the desert in an alien world while being hunted by 3 armed 3 eyed humanoid/bug monsters while creatures miles long fly above you.  I hope he writes more books set in this world beset by dimension problems and vengeful Elder Gods. While not required whatsoever, I think it does help to read 14 first--since it will help explain the ending, which if you haven't read the prior book would not make much sense whatsoever.

I'd like to choose my words carefully and avoid spoilery details but I'm not sure if that's possible... Let's see. 
 I very much enjoyed where Butcher went with post-ghost Dresden. There were multiple spots where I thought: sigh, it's going THAT way? when, BOOM! He takes it in a much better direction that maintains the characters' "humanity" and intelligence. I use humanity in quotes, because it's not always humans who are acting altruistically*. 
 My examples of some of those spots are behind the spoiler link... 
  Like when Dresden first came back to Chicago or first re-united with close friends/family like Molly, Thomas, and Murphy. I was worried it would start going down the road of overly dramatic, but it was handled nicely and kept them all emotionally connecting again but at the same time being smart about it and still focusing on the mission. Or when the Council or the White Court were mentioned, I was worried the plot would start to focus too much on their input restricting Dresden from really delving deeper into the faerie intrigue. But, whew did it delve. And the White Court and Council both pretty much remained out of scene. Or when Harry started to internally battle the Slate-Winter Court mantle, I started getting irritated that it was getting a little TOO internal. But for once it seems Butcher spares Harry some, and he continuously is able to maintain his own mentality. 
 But how badass was that scene with Mothers Winter and Summer and the gate. The faerie plot lines definitely are interesting me a lot more than the vampire ones, just seems like there's so much more to them. 
 And I was SO sad when the realization about Molly's fate came clear. I mean, it sounds like it might be ok but it's just sad, Molly doesn't deserve that. It's like Harry pissed off A LOT of people and eventually felt like he had no other choice but to take the mantle. But Molly hardly pissed off anyone and she's pretty much stuck with the same fate. 
 Ok, let's join the non-spoiler folks again... 
  
 I really felt warm and squishy near the end when shit had long since hit the fan and Dresden is about to invoke this big-pretty-much-uncontrollable energy and is asking himself what other choice does he have? When he realizes he has friends. I felt like that was huge for Harry's character. So many other times he takes power to the extreme regardless of the consequences because he wants to protect everyone and thinks he has to do it alone, but it sounds like it's finally sinking in that he can't do it alone and he's got friends to back him up. 
 * Although, thinking about it now with society the way it is, I'm not entirely sure if humanity is still an appropriate synonym for good morals and altruism...

 Isabella Cale has set up a nice life for herself in Scotland, with an imitation jewelry making business creating a profit and a daughter whom she adores. Everything is going rather smoothly until her husband shows back up. Ten years after he abandoned her, she wants nothing to do with him. After all, he helped her family steal royal jewels and then vanished with his share of the spoils. But when she sets eyes on him, he seems furious with her for setting him up and deserting him, which she most certainly did not do. Is there more to this story than the main two are aware of? Can they find their way back to each other? 
 Isa is the hardworking type of heroine that we don't see overly much in historical romances. Working women were shunned in that time period, so it's completely understandable that they were dependent on their husbands or fathers or various other relatives for their livelihood. After she was abandoned by her husband, she refused to continue living with her controlling sister and brother-in-law, not with the happiness of her future child hanging in the balance and she convinces a fellow imitation jewelry maker to become her partner in the business he was moving to Scotland. She has worked and toiled to build their business and is now considered a respectable woman. She has even caught the eye of a Baron, though she knows nothing but friendship will even come from it. She was strong and determined to protect her child, regardless of any consequences. 
 Victor, her husband, is the upstanding citizen that was left holding the bag after Isa's sister and brother-in-law made off with the jewels. Since there was never any concrete proof, he could not be hanged for the crime, but that doesn't mean they didn't interrogate and torture the poor fellow. He harbors such bitter rage over the theft and Isa's abandonment that it never even occurs to him that maybe she was just as much of a pawn as he was. He's not the most swoon-worthy HR hero I've read, but I definitely could sympathize with his situation. 
 This is my very favorite type of historical romance novel. Lies and misunderstandings separating our beloved couple and then smackdown confrontation and love when the two figure out they were mislead or duped. I love the dancing around each other trying not to reveal too much of their current situation while fighting the ever-present desire for each other. I love (love love) reading the confrontation where both parties learn of the deception and go all lovey-dovey because they realize they both are still in love. I love that whole bit. 
 Sabrina Jeffries has never been my favorite writer of this genre, but she is quickly gaining my respect. This novel in particular was intriguing and addictive, even if the love scenes were a bit mediocre. I found it impossible to put this book down, anxious to find out if Isa's sister (and brother-in-law) were going to find her and what would happen when they did. Also how Victor would take the news that he had a child he was unaware of. Sooo much drama, but the best kind of drama. The kind that keeps you coming back for more instead of rolling your eyes in exasperation. 
 I know I keep saying this, but I really must make reading these more of a priority. I know I love YA (and NA), but there is just something more magical about this particular genre. I don't know if it's the writer's talent or the setting or just the storyline itself, but reading these are my biggest comfort read. It's like slipping into an old pair of jeans that magically still fit perfectly even though you are not the same as you were when you were them in the past. You can find everything you'll ever need in a historical romance here and I highly recommend it to all my historical romance readers!

If you're looking for a good YA book to get yourself in the Halloween/Fall spirit, or just looking for a subtly creepy read, this is definitely the book for you! I found this novel to be very well structured from beginning to end. The plot moved slowly at first but I actually preferred it this way, as it allowed tension and suspense to build. It also gave the reader a chance to get to know the main character, Jacob, as well as establish more nuanced sub plots that would be revealed later, during the climax. 
 I actually loved the accompanying photographs of peculiar children that were woven throughout the book and felt that it helped me to immerse myself in the story. Finding out afterwards that the majority of the photographs used were authentic, caused me to second guess whether the story could be true, if only for a second. Minute details such as this really just separated this book for me and made it stand out above others. The photographs also allowed me to visualize and picture the world of Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children (MPHPC) in the time period that much of the novel is set in. 
 In trying to find a comparable story, I would have to say that MPHPC stands alone. I must admit that at first the thought crossed my mind that it was similar, in some ways, to X-Men, but after further consideration I found this not to be true. Here's why. Spoiler:  In MPHPC, the children are peculiar, yes, but not x-men crazy like superheroes, nor are they magical like wizards in Harry Potter. The other key difference that I found is that MPHPC is built around the concept of time travel. It's not just a minor event that rarely occurs, like in HP or X-Men; it's a central part of the story, and from what I can tell it will continue to be important during the rest of the series. Also, the children stay children and do not grow up, so long as they remain in their time loops. The world that Riggs has invented is not comparable to X-Men, Harry Potter, or any other novel that I'm aware of involving children with unique capabilities.  
 This book was definitely just creepy enough to cause the hairs on the back of my neck to stand while reading alone in my house at midnight. Such a thrill, great writing, and really good characters. The only reason I gave this book 4 stars instead of 5 is because I just didn't feel that it stands up with the rest of the books I've given 5 star ratings to, which include a lot of classics and books that have stood the test of time. I'll have to revisit this one in 30 years and see where it's at. 
 Tea pairing: Teavana's Oprah Chai Tea. Perfect fall flavours and subtly spicy, just like MPHPC.

Officially a Warden for the White Council, Harry has been struggling with his part in the actions the council takes out as part of their enforcement of the Laws of Magic. After the brutal execution of a young man in his city, Harry is tasked with tracking down the source of Black Magic which has been running through Chicago. 
 It's a task which soon takes him to SplatterCon!!!, sees his car being totalled, a re-introduction to a young Molly Carpenter and a battle in the heart of Winter. Oh and a KICK ASS Charity. 
 We also see the first confirmation of a foe which has been lurking in the background since the start of the series... the Black Council. 
 I'd actually forgotten until halfway through that this was the book where Molly's powers first start to manifest themselves and the judgement of the Council at the end. Very exciting.

A well written book that did not connect with my tastes. There's a lot here that matches up with my appeal factors: complex science fiction, interesting takes on post-humanity, and a twisty plot. But overall, the work left me flat. I was expecting more of a caper novel (with the emphasis on thievery). Instead, it's a lyrical work with a very Continental feel (i.e., the future Mars clearly shows strong French influences).

4 - 4 1/2 stars 
 I was pleasantly surprised by Requiem - I had glanced at a few reviews on Goodreads which hadn't filled me with a lot of confidence, which is the main reason I didn't rush to buy and read it immediately. I am pleased that I wasn't completely put off though, because this is a great season finale. Maybe not quite as amazing as finales like Clockwork Princess or Mockingjay, but still pretty awesome. 
 I love Oliver's writing style - the way that she constructs her sentences and lets ideas build within them - it creates a vivid yet personal first person narrative. I think that these books would be really great to read aloud in a reading group. 
 The quality of the writing has always been one of the big draws of the series for me and is probably why I will rush to buy whatever Oliver writes next. 
 What I love about dystopian novels is how different they all are and how individual and creative each series concept is. Reading the back cover of Delirium was one of those 'this is going to be amazing' moments and the series hasn't disappointed. 
 However, there was a couple of points at which I thought the concept could have gone a little further - some of the 'zombies' react more emotionally than I expect them to, which was particularly noticeable in Hanna's chapters. 
 It shouldn't come as a surprise to anyone who has read Fire that I like stories told from multiple perspectives, so I loved that we saw things from Hanna's POV in Requiem. I think that the story made more sense overall because of it and it was great to see the world Oliver has created from the perspective of someone who has been 'cured'. It provided more depth to the story and it was interesting to see important events described by the other side. 
 This next paragraph is all about the ending of the book and the love triangle, so don't read on if you haven't already read Requiem: 
  I have yet to read a series where the guy I was rooting for didn't win. Maybe I'm just lucky, or maybe I have a knack for picking the right one. Either way, I felt that this series was the closest I've got to thinking that my guy might not get the girl... I think that was probably the reason I couldn't put the book down - I had to know who Lena chose! For this reason, I am mostly happy with the way that Oliver chose to end the series, although there's definitely room for more happiness - it wasn't quite the happily ever after I had wanted which, in a series which is supposed to be all about love, was rather disappointing. Instead, Oliver focuses on dystopian themes of freedom and society and happiness, which is great and sticks well to her genre, but I don't feel that it accurately reflected the stand-out theme which made this series so different. However, it was still a much, much, much better ending than the Julian-centred alternative I had been panicking about, so I'm quite content overall. I also thought that the final paragraph was really powerful and an emphatic way to end.

Quick review: Think Malazan Book of the Fallen, but focusing only on the marines. Sounds good right? 
 Especially given the fact that MBotF is one of my all-time favorite series and the marines were always my favorite parts. Now don't get me wrong, I'm not saying I enjoyed this more, but I can't help but make the comparison and think it a good one. Don't ask me how my mind works, I obviously don't have a clue. 
 The comparison also makes sense because this series was influential on Erikson's MBotF. They're completely different, but the cynicism is definitely there in this mercenary band (I'm talking about The Black Company now) and it doesn't hold your hand as you're getting acquainted with the book. 
 As a big Malazan fan, I'm also a huge fan of authors that let you struggle. Authors that trust the intelligence of their readers, that they'll get it, they'll figure things out, and they'll be rewarded by it as well. 
 I think the part where The Black Company diverges quite a bit from the Malazan world is that where Malazan is vast, The Black Company is not. The limited viewpoint, following the first person account of Croaker (Crokus anyone?) who's both the company healer and historian, definitely holds back the worldbuilding, but I'm not complaining either. Just noting. And that's not to say it's not vast, you just don't get a sense of the world as much when you only follow a single person. I'm sure the world expands as the series progresses. 
 Overall, this was a really fun book. It's not black and white, you don't even really know if The Black Company is fighting for the right side, but that's what makes it good. They're just trying to make it through their commission. 
 Plus, there are some great, zany characters, like One-Eye and Goblin, who magically duel each other constantly, pranking each other with the most ridiculous things and then having more ridiculous things gobble up the previous ridiculous things. It's just great fun. 
 Croaker, the narrator as I mentioned, has a great voice. He takes his job seriously, but there's no pretense either. I can't wait to read more from the annals of the Black Company. 
 4 out of 5 Stars (highly recommended)

This was a quick, easy read and a nice addition to the Hashtag series. I'm glad that the first 100 pages or so focused on the night between Ivy and Braeden (I hate when there's a one-night stand but we don't get any of the details; typically the story just starts with the two MCs just avoiding each other or being snippy which I find annoying, so I was really glad that we got the full story here). I absolutely love Ivy! I thought her character was written really well and I'm excited to continue her story and see how she develops some more confidence and hopefully a backbone. I was really annoyed though at  how quickly she forgave Braeden after he called her a slut...especially since he didn't even apologize for it...that wasn't cool at all and I'm really disappointed by it . I also wish Ivy and Braeden had spent more time together by choice. There were a couple of "accidents" where they were kind of forced together, but other than that not many choice meetings until the very end...it would have been nice if they actively pursued each other a little more. 
 I was really impressed by how well the BuzzBoss storyline was written. I honestly was flipping between characters the entire time and I was glad that it was written in a way that didn't make it obvious, and I'm really excited to see how this reveal plays out in the next few books. The ending was absolute PERFECTION...it was adorable and is definitely satisfying while we wait on the next book!

This book is a perfect example of why I feel Goodreads should implement a half star system. I don't feel like this book deserves a 3, but it wasn't so bad that I'd give it a 2, either. The book featured characters I felt were a bit bland, and had very little character development to make them be more interesting. Unfortunately, this even applied to the main characters. I also felt there were way too many characters introduced in a short period of time, which made remembering who was who difficult. The pacing also seemed bad to me, as it was either too slow, or too fast. I also did not enjoy how quickly the Jinn was defeated. I feel that the battle should have been a bit longer, as defeating him seemed WAY too easy. There were some good points, however, which is why I feel it deserves a 2.5 or 3 verses a 2. I did enjoy the return of the Champions from the last book, and I thought Lyuba was a great character. She was the most interesting character in the book, and I wish she had been the protagonist instead. Her relationship with the guard(I don't remember his name) would have probably been more interesting to read about than what we were given.  I was really disappointed with this book. I loved the first two(especially One Good Knight), and had figured this one would be even better, or at least just as good as the other two. I'm really hoping The Snow Queen is better than this was. I don't want to ever have to give a Mercedes Lackey book a 3 again.

Amongst all the other problems of this truly terrible YA series, I don't know what Meyer was thinking when she decided that she was going to have the about to be born half-vampire baby break Bella's back and have Edward use his vampire teeth to chew through Bella's uterus to deliver it. It was surprise uncharacteristically explicit gory wtf-ness that I really did not expect from a YA book that is probably read by really young pre-teens because they think it's so romantic or whatever. Though since Meyer doesn't seem to understand that the relationships in Wuthering Heights weren't romantic in the least, and were in fact creepy and manipulative (which admittedly is an apt comparison to the unhealthy and slightly disturbing relationship Edward and Bella have), I guess I shouldn't have expected her to handle this demon baby pregnancy in any sort of way that makes sense.

Neil Gaiman's American Gods can be classified as mythology. Gaiman asks, "What happened to the gods of the people who came to America?" He offers a possible answer in the form of a story. Through the unusual adventures of Shadow, we learn that the older gods have competed for people's attention and generally lost out to the modern gods of technology, television, and even railroads. That is one way of looking at this book. One could also consider Shadow, his story, and what he represents. 
 American Gods is a complex story with many ideas contained within it. It would make an interesting book for a book club discussion. However, it also has language and a graphic sex scene (at least in the tenth anniversary addition) that will make it unsuitable for some.
Initially I was a little unsure of the ghost romance idea, but in this story it really worked for me. Cas was a really interesting main character and Anna... wow. Book 2 is going on my to-read list!
